item.content:encoded:
唐纳德·特朗普正在兑现他承诺的驱逐行动

简报 | 移民及海关执法局处境艰难 移民问题是唐纳德·特朗普的标志性议题——也是帮助他赢得竞选的关键之一。在2024年总统竞选期间，他承诺实施美国历史上最大规模的驱逐行动。这一誓言与他第二次竞选总统紧密相连，正如“修建边境墙”与他2016年首次竞选时密不可分。在选民投票前几天，麦迪逊广场花园的人群为特朗普欢呼，他吹嘘要围捕移民——他称其为“恶毒且嗜血的罪犯”——并“尽快将他们赶出我们的国家”。第二任期已过18个月，特朗普正在兑现他承诺的许多驱逐行动。国土安全部声称，在特朗普总统任期内已有约100万人被驱逐。实际数字可能低得多；政府停止发布官方统计数据，使得精确核算无从谈起。但即便如此，特朗普现在主持的驱逐机器与以往任何一届都不同，甚至超越了创下纪录的“驱逐总司令”巴拉克·奥巴马。考虑到今年年初的情况，这令人瞩目。1月份，联邦特工在明尼阿波利斯的移民突袭中杀害了两名美国公民，政府随即退缩。全国爆发抗议活动。明尼阿波利斯行动的军事化代表格雷戈里·博维诺被流放到加利福尼亚州并退休。国土安全部长克里斯蒂·诺姆被解职，国土安全部因国会围绕移民执法资金的争斗而关闭了76天。诺姆最终由俄克拉何马州共和党参议员马克韦恩·穆林接替，他在确认听证会上表示自己的目标是避免上新闻。边境巡逻特工不再从直升机上绳降至公寓楼，也不再随意向街上的抗议者投掷催泪瓦斯。 但从驱逐行动的宣传表演中撤退，并不等于从驱逐本身撤退。围绕移民执法的预算僵局在6月结束，共和党人集体投票决定再向移民及海关执法局和边境巡逻队提供700亿美元资金。此后，移民及海关执法局的移民逮捕人数急剧上升——6月达到43,000人，7月接近50,000人，这是特朗普上任以来最高的月度总数，也是该机构的纪录（见图表1）。 隶属司法部的移民法官正以有史以来最高的比率对移民发出驱逐令（见图表2）。超过160万移民现已被下达驱逐令，这意味着他们只需再遭遇一次移民及海关执法局就可能被驱逐出境。试图庇护邻居免受驱逐的活动人士称之为“暗影激增”。然而，即使以不那么公开对抗的形式出现，特朗普的大规模驱逐行动仍然比一些支持者预期的更加激进、新颖和残酷。部分原因在于特朗普正在执行的驱逐类型与以往截然不同。在2013财年，奥巴马政府驱逐了超过43万人，创下纪录，当时他主要针对近期越境者和罪犯。如今边境越境人数已降至最低，特朗普的驱逐行动主要发生在美国境内，目标是许多在美国生活多年的移民。他们可能与美国公民结婚，或拥有美国公民身份的子女。有些甚至是儿童。要开展这样的行动，需要更多街头对抗、更多长期拘留、更多驱逐航班。以及更多争议。许多守法的移民被卷入法网，导致家庭破碎，雇主受损。自特朗普就职以来，已有56人在移民及海关执法局拘留期间死亡，是拜登政府整个任期内死亡人数的两倍多；批评者称许多移民被关押在肮脏、过度拥挤的环境中。移民及海关执法局在残酷对待移民方面的名声几乎没有改善；本月有消息称，该机构计划花费高达2000万美元为特工配备可释放电击的手套。国土安全部还正在考虑为无人陪伴的儿童建造一个大型新拘留设施，并使得儿童更难找到律师在移民法庭上代表他们。不断有新闻报道称幼儿面临独自被驱逐或受到其他虐待。 所有这些都对特朗普政策的支持率造成了损害：超过五分之一的2024年特朗普选民现在支持废除移民及海关执法局，这一立场曾被视为极左组织口号而遭嘲笑（现在47%的美国人支持废除该机构，见图表3）。对特朗普行动的反弹可能会在中期选举中伤害共和党——从长远来看，可能导致移民制度的彻底改革。短期内，驱逐行动看起来将继续毫无松懈，只是在新领导层下不再那么喧嚣。无论在风格还是实质上，穆林似乎都是特朗普边境事务总管汤姆·霍曼的追随者。两人都是总统的忠实支持者和移民强硬派，但更关注执法效率而非炫耀性突袭。“我不会像前任部长那样处理事情，”穆林8月在俄克拉何马城对州长们说。“我们不做工作场所突袭。我们不会去家得宝停车场突袭。”民主党人和共和党人的州长告诉《经济学人》，自他掌舵以来，国土安全部对他们的回应更加积极。当马里兰州民主党州长、潜在的2028年总统候选人韦斯·摩尔拿起话筒时，穆林打趣道：“我和这家伙经常交谈。”穆林领导下的国土安全部已停止围攻民主党执政的城市。但街头逮捕移民的行动仍在继续。移民及海关执法局官员今年夏天告诉《纽约时报》，白宫要求每天逮捕2,000人。该机构尚未在一个月内维持如此高的执法水平，但积累数字的压力似乎已产生危险后果。7月，德克萨斯州和缅因州各有一名移民在交通拦停逮捕中被移民及海关执法局特工杀害。几天后，佛罗里达州有四人遭到移民特工接近。他们徒步逃跑；一人被卡车撞倒身亡。与此同时，政府通过采取新颖的法律策略，大幅扩大了可逮捕人群的范围，使至少170万移民新近面临被驱逐的风险。他们做到这一点的最直接方式是终止某些国籍人士的签证以及临时移民和人道主义计划。在拜登政府时期，南部边境挤满了希望申请庇护的人。为了减轻边境压力，乔·拜登总统扩大了部分移民合法入境或居留的替代法律选项，包括人道主义“假释”和临时保护身份（TPS）。TPS指定允许因母国遭受自然或政治灾难而滞留在美国的某些国籍人士在一段时间内合法工作和居住。特朗普政府系统性地拆除了这些保护措施，以及其他已实施数十年的保护措施。“我们中的许多人在2022年就警告过他们，我们放进来的人以后会非常脆弱，”曾在奥巴马和拜登政府期间从事移民政策工作的安德里亚·弗洛雷斯说。总的来说，法院对特朗普的驱逐行动起到了推波助澜的作用。6月，最高法院裁定政府可以终止对来自叙利亚和海地的TPS持有者的保护。来自13个国家的超过100万人现已失去TPS。他们中许多人无法再工作，面临法院命令的驱逐——而且与一些无证移民不同，他们尤其暴露在风险中，因为政府确切知道他们在哪里。“所有TPS终止现已生效，”国土安全部在社交媒体平台X上发帖称。“被终止TPS的人应立即离开。如果不离开，我们将驱逐他们。”另有17万萨尔瓦多TPS持有者将在9月失去身份；其中一些已在美国生活了25年。特朗普对某些TPS持有者的执念可以追溯到多年前。在2024年与卡玛拉·哈里斯的总统辩论中，他声称俄亥俄州斯普林菲尔德的海地人“在吃当地居民的宠物”（实际上没有）。7月，移民及海关执法局开始命令俄亥俄州中部海地人向哥伦布当地外勤办公室报到，在那里他们被戴上脚踝监视器——据报道此前他们被邀请自行离境。“当然没人接受，”全国倡导组织海地桥梁联盟的格尔琳·约瑟夫说。海地大部分地区被帮派控制，暴力横行。约瑟夫女士表示，被驱逐到该国“可能是死刑判决”。近年来，遣返海地的航班有所减少，但并未停止。2026年每月有一架次从路易斯安那州飞往海地角的航班。 不仅仅是前TPS持有者突然变得脆弱。政府还搅乱了官僚程序，使许多移民——包括签证续签和绿卡申请人——陷入法律困境。（待处理的移民申请数量已达到惊人的1,130万件。）联邦特工最近也加大了对签证过期移民在机场的逮捕力度。根据监督组织“美国监督”获得的文件，此类逮捕之所以可能，是因为移民及海关执法局与运输安全管理局正在更紧密地合作。一些在试图乘机时被拘留的人被困在漫长的身份调整排队中。穆林坚称，遵守规则但陷入法律困境的移民不会被驱逐。“如果你正在走家庭签证系统，没有犯罪记录，你被抓住了，而且……你一直按时出庭，”他在俄克拉何马城说，“你会被释放的。”如果移民不相信他的话，也是情有可原的。国土安全部还在使用人工智能帮助寻找可逮捕的人。与移民及海关执法局有长期合作关系的科技公司Palantir向政府提供了一种名为ELITE的工具。根据法庭证词，使用ELITE的特工可以生成一份“目标名单”，附有照片和姓名，显示移民可能居住的地方。“这有点像谷歌地图，”一名特工说。“如果一栋房子上只有一个图钉，而且他们实际住在那里的可能性只有10%，你不会去那里。”一旦被移民及海关执法局带走，移民便会被以疯狂的速度推过移民法庭。法官们正在举行所谓的“超级大庭”以尽快处理案件。追踪移民记录的非营利组织“移动通道”将“超级大庭”定义为一次审理超过50个案件的听证会。该组织在6月统计到超过1,300场此类听证会。最近一个周五，在洛杉矶市中心，杰米·哈索法官在三个小时的听证会上审理了96个案件。其中大多数仅持续不到五分钟。他的目光时常瞟向时钟，始终注意着时间。法庭一名书记员表示，每位法官每周举行一次超级大庭，移民及其家属挤满了外面的走廊。许多移民没有按时出庭——要么担心案件审结后会被逮捕，要么越来越多地是因为没有收到充分的听证变更通知。一名无法联系到客户的律师告诉哈索法官，她不确定客户是否还在美国。当移民未能出庭时，国土安全部律师会请求法院“缺席”下达驱逐令。根据“移动通道”的数据，这成为7月份超过三分之一案件的结果。缺席的人越多，政府可以累积的驱逐令就越多。特朗普的大规模驱逐行动可能针对的是移民，但它也对美国的法治产生了更广泛的影响。移民及海关执法局和边境巡逻队特工袭击抗议者却不受惩罚，并试图以可疑的说辞逮捕一些声称曾将汽车用作武器的人。当蒙面、无身份标识的官员在没有警告的情况下将移民塞进无标记车辆时，这看起来像绑架。数千名联邦特工已从反恐或毒品走私等其他调查工作中抽调出来支援移民及海关执法局。地方执法人员，包括坚定的保守派，担心激进策略可能会更广泛地侵蚀对警察的信任。“你不能进入社区开始投掷闪光弹……然后期望成功，”亚利桑那州一位县警长马克·丹内尔斯说。由于丹内尔斯与政府关系密切，他说，几位警长打电话向他抱怨。许多警察部门也曾努力赢得移民社区的信任，说服无证移民相信他们可以安全地举报犯罪。这项工作已被摧毁。 总体而言，特朗普驱逐行动的粗糙边缘和纯粹残酷性开始重塑政治格局。美国人对总统移民议程的态度已大幅转冷（见图表4）。根据《经济学人》/YouGov的民意调查，8月他在移民问题上的净支持率降至-13。在西班牙裔中——他们的支持帮助特朗普在2024年获胜——他对移民处理的净支持率是灾难性的-35。约55%的西班牙裔支持废除移民及海关执法局，比白人或黑人美国人高出十个百分点。民主党人正瞄准几个目前由共和党占有的西班牙裔占多数的众议院席位，包括南德克萨斯州的四个。然而，美国的移民政治可能只会变得更加有毒。大规模驱逐在特朗普的基本盘中仍然受欢迎：93%认同MAGA的共和党人赞成总统的移民处理方式。“大规模驱逐联盟”的创始人迈克·豪厄尔认为更高的逮捕数字并不令人印象深刻。该组织是在明尼阿波利斯“南境大行动”后成立的，旨在敦促政府坚持下去。“他们仍然很低，”他说。“关键是要去人口密集的地方，然后，你知道，在那里抓人。”他希望大规模驱逐的支持能成为未来每场共和党初选的试金石。事实上，MAGA共和党人将穆林较少对抗的方式视为懦弱的退缩。特朗普的前首席策略师史蒂夫·班农和其他MAGA影响者主张更换他。穆林已意识到需要巩固MAGA基本盘。8月，在向州长们发表了一番听起来合理的评论（称某些行业确实需要移民工人）之后，他在X上发帖跟进：“对非法移民绝不赦免。永远不。”民主党人可能也正走向一场关于移民执法的党内斗争。尽管现在明显多数的民主党人支持废除移民及海关执法局，但党内许多坚定分子担心在这个问题上听起来过于激进，会疏远仍然支持强边境安全的广大选民。一些民主党和共和党温和派希望，特朗普的残酷行为，加上包括拜登时期在内的长期失败边境政策历史，已暴露出移民改革的必要性。国会自1990年代以来未通过任何有意义的移民方案。“我见过我们尝试又失败，尝试又失败，接近成功又失败，我认为如果你看看不解决这个问题对我们国家的影响，那是巨大的，”犹他州共和党参议员约翰·柯蒂斯承认。具有讽刺意味的是，20年来，主要是共和党人，包括特朗普本人，阻止了移民改革，助长了使特朗普反移民言论如此受欢迎的政治环境。 如今约一半美国人支持增加边境安全投资并限制可申请庇护的移民数量。但更大比例的美国人也支持为以下无证移民提供入籍途径：小时候抵达的、与美国公民结婚的、在美国居住至少十年的、或有美国子女的（见图表5）。这些都是特朗普正在围捕的那类移民。至少一些在集会人群中热烈欢呼特朗普的人似乎开始意识到，他所兑现的驱逐行动并不是他们想要的那一个。■

item.title: Australia builds a Pacific alliance system to keep China out
item.description:
Asia

Asia | Pushing back THE GRAND PACIFIC HOTEL is an old British colonial institution at the heart of Fiji’s capital. Tropical breezes blow off the harbour and through its whitewashed verandas to parliament across the street. On July 6th Fiji’s prime minister was hosting a banquet there for his Au...
item.content:encoded:
Australia builds a Pacific alliance system to keep China out

Asia | Pushing back


THE GRAND PACIFIC HOTEL is an old British colonial institution at the heart of Fiji’s capital. Tropical breezes blow off the harbour and through its whitewashed verandas to parliament across the street. On July 6th Fiji’s prime minister was hosting a banquet there for his Australian counterpart to celebrate a new mutual-defence pact between their two countries. They had just signed the treaty when word reached them that a Chinese submarine would shortly test-launch a ballistic missile into international waters north of Fiji. The test was only the second Chinese launch since 1980 of a ballistic missile into international waters. It spooked leaders of Pacific island countries, including Fiji, whose defence minister had unsuccessfully urged China to call it off, and some of whose soldiers are pictured above.

For Fiji and several other Pacific island countries it was the latest in a series of Chinese actions that have convinced them they have been right to align more closely with Australia. Their concern about the missile launch is born of their history. Bigger countries turned the Pacific into a battleground in the second world war and into a testing ground for nuclear weapons during the cold war. (Both the July test and an earlier one in September 2024, which also landed in the Pacific, were of nuclear-capable missiles.) Now, many Pacific island leaders fear that rivalry between America and Asia’s biggest military power will once again destabilise their region.

Rather than choose between America and China, however, Pacific leaders are choosing to deepen ties with Australia by signing the Asia-Pacific’s first new alliances since the early days of the cold war. The mutual-defence treaty between Australia and Fiji, the Pacific islands’ commercial and diplomatic hub, is the second new military alliance that Australia has signed with a Pacific island state in less than a year. It did a similar deal with the region’s biggest state, Papua New Guinea, in October 2025. Negotiations with Tonga, now the only Pacific island country with defence forces that does not have an alliance with Australia, are under way. (Australia and New Zealand have been allies since the early days of the cold war.)

Ministers insist the deals are not about confronting China, but about keeping security arrangements within the “Pacific family”. That means Australia and New Zealand, which have long been members of the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), the regional organisation. It makes room, too, for America, which has sole responsibility for the defence of three states that are members of the PIF (and two heavily fortified territories, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, that are not). But it would lock China out of the region’s security arrangements. That is a big shift from just a few years ago, when Australian officials feared that China had the momentum, and was within reach of realising its ambition of a military base in the islands.

All of this adds up to a new system of military alliances among Pacific island countries. For the moment that system looks like a smaller version of the hub-and-spoke model of America’s alliances in Asia. Unlike in Europe, where NATO is a multilateral alliance, America has only bilateral alliances with its five treaty allies in Asia. Likewise, Australia now has three bilateral alliances in the Pacific.

But that could soon change. New Zealand has expressed an interest in also signing the Veitacini Treaty, as the new alliance between Australia and Fiji is known. If it follows through, probably only after elections in New Zealand in November, the pact could become the basis for a new multilateral alliance in the Pacific, say officials in all three countries. “A bit like a NATO, kind of,” modestly offers Fiji’s deputy prime minister, Manoa Kamikamica, in an interview in his office in Suva, the capital.

The alliance is open only to those countries that have defence forces, however. For those that don’t, Australia offers other deals. Agreements with Tuvalu in 2023 and Vanuatu in June would block China from building military bases there and make it harder to do security deals dressed up as police co-operation. The Solomon Islands, for the past several years China’s closest Pacific ally, is negotiating a similar agreement with Australia after a change in government in May. Of the region’s other fully independent states, only two—Kiribati and Samoa—have yet to conclude a treaty with Australia or open negotiations.

Both the defence pacts and the other treaties discourage Chinese investment in critical infrastructure that could have military uses, like ports or telecommunication networks. In return, Australia is investing more than $1bn each year in its new treaty partners. In Fiji Australian diplomats hope to get the Millennium Challenge Corporation, an American aid agency that Elon Musk and DOGE forgot to destroy last year, to add several hundred million dollars for redeveloping Suva’s strategically located deepwater port.

Matthew Wale, the new prime minister of the Solomons and a longtime critic of China’s attempts to buy influence in the region, wants all Pacific island countries, whether they have defence forces or not, to agree on a new multilateral treaty limiting security co-operation to the “Pacific family” at their annual summit, which begins on August 30th. But approval would require consensus between all of the forum’s members. For two of the bloc’s weakest states, Kiribati and Nauru, that may go too far towards alienating China. The two have also blocked a statement condemning the Chinese missile launch, to the dismay of the other members. Nauru opposed the protest despite the treaty it signed with Australia in 2024.

Much of the discussion avoids the fact that by choosing Australia, an American ally, Pacific leaders are choosing sides. There is little talk in Fiji or the other treaty signatories of what an Australian ally might be asked to do if Australia joined America in a conflict with China. And military co-operation between Australia and its new allies will proceed slowly; there is, for example, little prospect of Australian troops deploying permanently on its new allies’ territory any time soon. That does not bother American officials, however, who are happy that Australian diplomacy seems to be blocking a Chinese presence in Pacific island countries that were once crucial territories in the battles of the second world war. ■

For exclusive coverage of Asian politics, economics and security, sign up to Asia Bulletin, our weekly subscriber-only newsletter.

item.title: Can AI make dysfunctional governments more effective?
item.description:
Asia

Asia | ChatGOV in Asia HOW MANY laws and regulations are needed to govern an archipelago, home to 287m people, spread across some 13,500 islands, and stretching more than 5,000km? For Indonesia, the answer is 251,232. Yet all too often this bureaucratic morass only worsens persistent problems, ...
item.content:encoded:
Can AI make dysfunctional governments more effective?

Asia | ChatGOV in Asia


HOW MANY laws and regulations are needed to govern an archipelago, home to 287m people, spread across some 13,500 islands, and stretching more than 5,000km? For Indonesia, the answer is 251,232. Yet all too often this bureaucratic morass only worsens persistent problems, from rampant graft to sluggish growth.

Indonesia is a vivid example of a challenge common to Asia’s populous poorer countries. Governments need to manage complex economies and provide services to diverse societies with limited resources. Officials across the region have long turned to digital technology for help making their operations more transparent and effective. Yet Indonesia has launched more than 27,000 digital public-sector platforms and apps, to little avail. Now they hope artificial intelligence can do better.

AI models could help boost the very capabilities that poor states often lack. They are adept at analysing lots of data, from tax filings to farm yields, at a relatively low cost. Properly adapted to local conditions, AI could allow developing countries to do “in a decade what might otherwise take a century”, the World Bank argues.

Public-sector experimentation with AI in poorer parts of Asia has so far been promising, albeit limited. Consider the courts in Pakistan, which face a backlog of more than 2m cases. In 2024 trial-court judges were given access to JudgeGPT, a generative-AI assistant grounded in Pakistani statutes and court judgments. The tool helped judges with legal research, summarising and drafting. Those who used it cleared around 6.3% more cases a year. Greater speed did not mean lower quality: appeal rates did not increase. Similarly, in India, where there is an even bigger legal logjam, Adalat AI, a startup, claims that its transcription tools and document-processing software have reduced case times by 30-50% across 11 Indian states.

The biggest gains may come from helping governments make better predictions, says Indermit Gill, the World Bank’s chief economist. Rampant theft and poor infrastructure make it hard for electrical utilities in poor countries to estimate demand. AI can help them take giant leaps, says Mohak Mangal, the co-founder of Pravah, a startup that is helping utilities in six Indian states deliver power more efficiently. In Telangana, a southern Indian state, a recent study found that AI-enhanced monsoon forecasts helped farmers reap savings of as much as 42,000 rupees ($560) in a cropping season, the equivalent of three months’ minimum wage in the region.

Overloaded officials hope AI can help meet a perennial challenge, directing welfare benefits more accurately. For example, a big food-assistance programme the Indonesian government runs reaches less than 50% of its intended recipients, according to SMERU Research Institute, a local think-tank. One pilot project in Banyuwangi, a port town in eastern Java, used AI to analyse data from different government databases to help verify recipients’ eligibility; a government-commissioned study found that the new system reduced the time taken to register recipients from 75-200 days to less than one. The government hopes to roll out the initiative to the rest of the country by the end of the year.

But wider adoption poses risks. Poverty can be dynamic, specific to local conditions and difficult to quantify, point out researchers at SMERU. More than 9,000 households challenged the AI’s initial categorisation in Banyuwangi. Researchers in Bangladesh tested whether a machine-learning model trained on mobile-phone use could examine data on phone top-ups, call patterns and mobility to improve the targeting of a cash-transfer programme. Only 32% of the households it identified were eligible, so more than two-thirds of the programme’s funds went to households that should not have received them.

Such findings point to the bigger challenge poor countries face when deploying AI: the places that could most use the technology to supplement state capacity are the same places that lack capacity to deploy the technology safely and effectively, and to develop models of their own. In a World Bank survey of officials from nearly 60 countries, around 80% of those from lower-income countries said they had no tools, or only basic ones, for evaluating the performance of their AI experiments.

Governments may not like the idea of running essential public services on technology controlled by foreign powers, yet most poor countries must rely on frontier models developed in America or China. The World Bank recommends using interoperable systems drawing on suppliers from different countries and starting by adapting simpler models to local conditions. Mr Gill thinks parts of Asia, such as India’s southern states and countries in South-East Asia, are well placed to do so.

To succeed, poorer states will need to focus on less glamorous back-end processes. This includes basics such as improving data quality, training officials and procuring technology sensibly, says Shahrukh Wani, who heads AI partnerships at the International Growth Centre, a British research institute. JudgeGPT is a case in point: the striking gains appeared only when access to the model was accompanied by targeted training on how to use it; when judges were handed the tool alongside a generic legal course, they were no more productive than before. Unless states lay the groundwork, AI could end up only deepening the bureaucratic morass. ■

For exclusive coverage of Asian politics, economics and security, sign up to Asia Bulletin, our weekly subscriber-only newsletter.

item.title: A hundred days of BJP shock and awe in West Bengal
item.description:
Asia

Asia | Culture clash FOR MANY years the Hindu nationalists’ student group at Jadavpur University in Kolkata was so unpopular that it imported middle-aged activists to pad out its rallies. But in May the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the party led by Narendra Modi, the prime minister, won West B...
item.content:encoded:
A hundred days of BJP shock and awe in West Bengal

Asia | Culture clash


FOR MANY years the Hindu nationalists’ student group at Jadavpur University in Kolkata was so unpopular that it imported middle-aged activists to pad out its rallies. But in May the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the party led by Narendra Modi, the prime minister, won West Bengal, the state that has Kolkata as its capital. For days in August emboldened students assaulted leftist rivals and torched their flags and posters. A minister urged more such “surgical strikes”. “They have the muscle power and the money power,” complains a 19-year-old political-science major, “and now they will start controlling this campus.”

Until now, West Bengal has been everything the Hindu-nationalist BJP is not: secular, left-leaning and abysmal at business. So victory for the party, its first-ever in the state, was especially sweet. But the mismatch also makes West Bengal among the biggest headaches the BJP has had to cope with in its 12 years of ruling India. The party promised big changes in its first 100 days, which expired on August 17th. But it has found waging culture wars is easier than fixing the economy.

For decades Communists and the Trinamool Congress, a regional party, ran West Bengal in fairly similar style. Their appetite for bribes and aversion to business reduced what was once one of India’s industrial strongholds to a “syndicate raj” of dodgy influence-peddling. May’s election unseated Trinamool’s Mamata Banerjee, a three-term chief minister and a fierce critic of Mr Modi. Many did not vote for the BJP so much as against her party’s corruption and thuggery.

After decades of bad blood between state and centre, things are smoother now . Infrastructure projects that were stalled are moving, including an extension to Kolkata’s metro system. Since the election, Delhi has pledged 1trn rupees (about $10.5bn) for railway projects in West Bengal. But winning over private-sector investors is a slow and thankless task. “I am on a hunt for one huge, iconic investment,” says Swapan Dasgupta, a maverick intellectual now serving as the state’s finance minister. One coup would be persuading Tata Group, India’s biggest conglomerate, to return with a big manufacturing project—two decades after Ms Banerjee staged a hunger strike and drove a planned Tata car factory out of the state.

The sweet talk is saved for businesses: the new government seems brazen about imposing an alien culture of Hindu nationalism on secular-minded, meat-loving Bengalis. “I will work for the Hindus,” announced Suvendu Adhikari, the new chief minister of a population that is close to 30% Muslim. The BJP has cleared Muslims at prayer from public roads and made it harder to sell halal meat. In a rush to deport “illegal infiltrators”, even some Indian citizens who happen to be Muslim have been pushed across the border into Muslim-majority Bangladesh. A brief attempt to remove eggs from midday meals in schools outraged many Hindus, who eschew the “pure” vegetarianism preferred by the Hindu nationalists of the north. Though many voters complain that Ms Banerjee coddled her Muslim vote-bank, few want the government to mess with West Bengal’s syncretic culture.

The BJP has also co-opted much of the opposition. In the national parliament in Delhi, 20 out of 28 Trinamool politicians have defected to Mr Modi’s coalition. In the state assembly, 65 of 80 Trinamool representatives have distanced themselves from Ms Banerjee as part of a breakaway faction that keeps suspiciously quiet on the BJP. Many, say critics, did so to ward off investigations by central law-enforcement agencies. One Banerjee loyalist was found hanging from the ceiling of the party office on August 16th, with a suicide note begging his family never to get into politics.

The BJP is rushing to show results in West Bengal before the next national election, expected in 2029. Because about 57% of state revenues come from Delhi, fixing the economy by such a tight deadline means that West Bengal must stay at the top of the national government’s list of priorities. The second challenge stems from the BJP’s decision to strengthen its presence in the state by inducting scores of high-profile Trinamool politicians into its ranks. These turncoats, including some tainted by corruption scandals, make it harder to convince voters and financiers that the state really has turned a page. ■

Stay on top of our India coverage by signing up to Essential India, our free weekly newsletter.

item.title: Indian cities should embrace skyscrapers
item.description:
Asia

Asia | Ashoka DONALD TRUMP’S popularity may be plummeting in America and around the world, yet India’s appetite for buildings bearing his name remains undiminished. This month a local developer licensing the Trump name announced the details of the latest such project. Promising “every comfort, ...
item.content:encoded:
Indian cities should embrace skyscrapers

Asia | Ashoka


DONALD TRUMP’S popularity may be plummeting in America and around the world, yet India’s appetite for buildings bearing his name remains undiminished. This month a local developer licensing the Trump name announced the details of the latest such project. Promising “every comfort, convenience and indulgence” and spread across two towers of 65 storeys each, it will be the country’s largest Trump-branded property. But those who are expecting to find this monument to the tastes of India’s new rich in high-rise Mumbai, brand-obsessed Delhi or tech-fuelled Bangalore will be disappointed. The home of the newest Trump towers is, surprisingly, Hyderabad.

The capital of the wealthy southern state of Telangana, Hyderabad is little known outside India. Domestically its reputation rests on its distinct culture (it serves as a meeting point for north and south India), wonderful cuisine (it produces the best biryani known to humanity, no matter what those misguided souls in Lucknow tell you) and thriving tech industry (Google, Microsoft and Amazon all have huge offices there). It is not famous for skyscrapers. Yet it has more of them than any Indian city bar Mumbai, which was forced into vertical growth by its island geography.

How did the country’s sixth-most populous city build its second-largest concentration of tall buildings? It got out of the way. Near the top of the long list of things holding India’s cities back is something called “floor space index” (FSI), or the ratio of permissible built-up area to land area. In successful Asian cities like Singapore, FSI is set as high as 25, meaning that for every square foot of land, a developer can build up to 25 square feet of tower. In India local authorities worried about meagre civic infrastructure set the number somewhere around 2. It rarely exceeds 4. The central government’s latest economic survey describes restrictive FSI as a distortion responsible for urban low-rise sprawl. Worse, the finance ministry’s economists write, it “raises land values and creates artificial scarcity in core urban areas”. Hyderabad, unique among India’s cities, abolished FSI in 2006.

And then, miraculously, life went on. NIMBYs foretell all sorts of doom the moment anyone talks about building anything. They warn of Gothamesque ghettos with gridlocked streets, dry taps and overflowing sewers. Nonsense. Today tall residential blocks line the highways in Hyderabad’s western suburbs and traffic still flows faster than in most major Indian cities. Dozens more towers, including the Trump ones, are sprouting in a neighbourhood called Kokapet that was not long ago full of custard-apple orchards and is now a forest of construction cranes.

There are two reasons Hyderabad has not descended into dystopia. One is its 160km-long orbital motorway, the first bit of which opened in 2008 and is now an arterial road in the new skyscraper belt. The other is that abolishing the arbitrary cap on FSI did not mean the abandonment of all rules. Regulations covering minimum street widths and required setbacks still apply. Aviation authorities impose restrictions around air-traffic funnels. The effect is that developers can build high only if they have a large enough plot next to a wide enough street somewhere far enough from an airport. Markets decide the rest. The cost of construction rises with height, so a builder’s decision about how much to pay for land and how tall to go rests on whether potential buyers of flats will cough up enough to make the project profitable. That has prevented a housing bubble.

The lesson for other Indian cities is not “abolish FSI”—or not just that, at any rate. It is that civic administrators should think about what purpose their cherished rules serve, and whether better designed policies can achieve those goals. Hyderabad’s stewards—across parties and across decades—had the uncommon wisdom to anticipate both the problems and the opportunities breakneck growth would bring, and to plan accordingly.

The results are plain. Mumbai is in the midst of an infrastructure boom that its residents and businesses agree should have happened half a century ago. Delhi’s now-decades-old metro transformed the city. Bangalore, India’s foremost tech hub, is still an embarrassing morass of ugly sprawl, poor roads and interminable commutes. Hyderabad, which covets its tech crown and is rare in having planned ahead, is a sleek, modern city that looks the way Bangalore should. ■

item.title: 中国国家的长臂
item.description:
China

中国 | 法律战，而非口水战 在中国共产党长期以官方话语讲述中国故事时所滋养的种种不满中，外国列强的治外法权滥用显得尤为突出。19世纪，殖民列强拒绝在他们控制的中国口岸遵守中国法律。21世纪，美国则通过制裁和出口管制，将其意志强加于境外，针对那些不讨其欢心的国家。因此，中国如今想要加入治外法权的游戏，并以愈发高涨的热情发动法律战，就格外引人注目。一个显著的例子发生在今年4月，中国下令拥有Facebook的Meta公司撤销其以20亿美元收购总部设在新加坡的人工智能初创公司Manus的交易。Meta遵从了，Manus的中国创始人也同样遵从，他们已被禁止离开中国。如果说这起事件带有某种法律即兴操作...
item.content:encoded:
中国国家的长臂

中国 | 法律战，而非口水战 在中国共产党长期以官方话语讲述中国故事时所滋养的种种不满中，外国列强的治外法权滥用显得尤为突出。19世纪，殖民列强拒绝在他们控制的中国口岸遵守中国法律。21世纪，美国则通过制裁和出口管制，将其意志强加于境外，针对那些不讨其欢心的国家。因此，中国如今想要加入治外法权的游戏，并以愈发高涨的热情发动法律战，就格外引人注目。一个显著的例子发生在今年4月，中国下令拥有Facebook的Meta公司撤销其以20亿美元收购总部设在新加坡的人工智能初创公司Manus的交易。Meta遵从了，Manus的中国创始人也同样遵从，他们已被禁止离开中国。如果说这起事件带有某种法律即兴操作的味道，那么中国政府现在正在制定法律，以加强对人工智能技术流动的控制。此外，自9月起，对个人实施出入境禁令的强化权力也将生效。这些只是一系列旨在将中国影响力延伸至境外的法律措施中的最新一批。这些措施范围广泛，涉及从外国制裁到民族政策等方方面面。它们标志着中国的急剧转向——中国长期以来一直反感美国的法律触角。美国法院能够追究企业（和个人）在国外的行为，很大程度上要归功于美国对全球金融体系的主导权。就中国自身的长臂是对他国制裁的报复而言，它的力量来源于中国对全球供应链的主导地位。但中国在境外发动法律战，也是为了加强国内的政治控制。这一急剧转向来自最高层。2018年，中国领导人习近平敦促党内官员“运用法律武器”，以匹配中国作为大国的地位。那年晚些时候，华为高管、这家电信巨头创始人之女孟晚舟应美国要求，在加拿大被捕，罪名是涉嫌隐瞒了在美国制裁下与伊朗客户的关系。新加坡管理大学的高亨利认为，孟晚舟被捕事件让中国警惕的领导人看到，关键企业及其员工在美国的算计面前多么脆弱。（中国的回应是以捏造的罪名逮捕两名加拿大人，并将他们扣为人质近三年。）中国第一部阻止企业遵守外国制裁（尤其是美国制裁）的法律于2021年出台。此后，中共将治外法权条款编织进大量新立法中。例如，2024年底发布的法规要求使用中国投入品的外国企业遵守中国的出口法律；还赋予北京官员审查外国企业客户的权力。这类似于美国的“外国直接产品规则”，华盛顿当局曾引用该规则限制荷兰制造的芯片制造设备流向中国。同样与美国相似，中国也开始对外国政客实施制裁。中国针对外国制裁的法律于今年4月更新，其模板是欧盟自身的“阻断法规”。该法规规定，欧盟企业和个人遵守欧盟视为非法的制裁属于违法。如果说有区别的话，中国的法律走得更远。它规定，任何外国企业遵守歧视中国实体的制裁均属违法。根据这些新法律，美国两大银行集团摩根大通和花旗集团正因按照美国财政部的命令冻结一家被制裁中国石油贸易商的资产，而在中国法院被起诉，合计索赔4400万美元。6月，最高人民法院在一起判决中援引新法律，裁定一家新加坡公司因拒绝为一家被制裁的香港公司运送电子产品货物而败诉。中国的举动让外国企业陷入困境，它们被迫选择遵守谁的法律。5月，伦敦和重庆（中国西南部）的法院在韩国巨头三星与中国电信设备制造商中兴通讯之间的许可纠纷中作出了截然不同的裁决。伦敦法官认定三星应支付中兴通讯约3.92亿美元，而中国法院则认定中兴通讯应获得接近两倍的金额。满足一家法院可能意味着违抗另一家。对三星来说，不承认重庆法院判决的后果可能比违抗英国法院更严重。像三星这样的大型跨国企业对中国有深度敞口，中国既是它们的市场，也是关键商品的供应方。乔治城大学法律中心的马克·贾表示，中国的长臂依赖的是冷酷而切实的筹码。中国的长臂还着眼于控制那些被视为威胁国家国内安全的个人和组织——这一概念的定义极其宽泛。7月，一部“促进民族团结”的法律生效；它将任何“破坏国家统一”的境外行为定为犯罪。目前提交全国人民代表大会（中国的橡皮图章议会）审议的一部网络犯罪法案，将把在境外托管或传输损害中国“公共利益”的信息定为犯罪。另一部正在审议的法律将把在中国境外实体收集腐败证据的权力成文化。近年来的许多法律法规都正式化并强化了国家在世界各地的现有强制触角，这包括绑架批评政权的中国公民，以及运营旨在部分监控和控制海外华人行为的秘密警察站。中共在海外广泛开展的统战活动也长期致力于增强其影响力、左右海外华人社群并消解对中国的批评。人权观察组织的亚尔昆·乌卢约尔表示，这一立法推动反映了集中控制的愿望；将规则成文化有助于强化官僚手段。贾补充说，通过将报复外国制裁的权力赋予自身，国家向外界传递了决心的信号。中国匆忙进行的域外立法中很大一部分，包括关于民族团结的条款，实际上关乎中共长期以来对维护内部稳定的执念。但其法律触角的不断延伸，在很大程度上揭示了习近平领导下中国塑造更合心意的外部环境的雄心——在这个环境中，中国不再是世界历史的受害者，而是世界历史的创造者。■ 订阅者可注册我们的新周报《 Drum Tower》，以了解世界如何看待中国，以及中国如何看待世界。

item.title: China’s latest cash cow is a clunky cartoon bull
item.description:
China

China | Film-going frenzy TO MANY grown-ups, the cartoon film “Niu Lai” would be 86 minutes of torture. Yet in recent days cinemas across China have been packed with older audiences happily enduring its crudely animated depiction of a bullock’s dream about motherly love and threatening predator...
item.content:encoded:
China’s latest cash cow is a clunky cartoon bull

China | Film-going frenzy


TO MANY grown-ups, the cartoon film “Niu Lai” would be 86 minutes of torture. Yet in recent days cinemas across China have been packed with older audiences happily enduring its crudely animated depiction of a bullock’s dream about motherly love and threatening predators. No matter that the film is excruciatingly slow-paced, with long seconds of silence as its characters merely blink. On a typical day in late August earnings at the box office were the seventh highest in China, just behind a new Hollywood blockbuster, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day”. The cartoon has become a meme-driven frenzy.

Western audiences have turned trashy films into cult classics: “The Room”, an American film released in 2003, became so notorious for its bad acting and appalling script and set design that audiences flocked to see it for laughs. “Niu Lai”, which is the bullock’s name (it means “the bull is coming”), has a similar attraction: a copy of it on YouTube, apparently filmed in a Chinese cinema with a mobile phone, drew more than 1.1m views before being deleted. The chuckles of the Chinese audience (the film is not supposed to be funny) are clearly audible.

Yet in a country where, unlike in Western countries, the government plays a big role in making, financing and shaping the narratives of films, the popularity of “Niu Lai”—an independent production by a mother-and-son team on a shoestring budget—is a remarkable phenomenon. Young people have flooded China’s social media with comments that often go beyond mere catcalling. On Weibo, one of the most popular platforms, posts with the hashtag “Niu Lai” have been viewed more than 170m times: well over the count (100m) for the hashtag of China’s currently hottest movie: “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East”. That one is a big-budget state-backed film that officials have been organising people to watch because of its heart-warming tale of a Chinese cook’s heroism amid a destructive American invasion of an Iraq-like country.

Despite deliberate seat-packing, the number-one film does appear to be genuinely popular. But online commenters use “Niu Lai” in order to poke at the industry’s pouring money into films that aim to spread the Communist Party’s messages; they use star actors but are often second-rate. Viewers carp at online censors’ habit of suppressing negative views of these party-backed extravaganzas. “Anyone can point at ‘Niu Lai’ and call it trash,” wrote one Weibo user to his more than 1.5m followers, echoing a commonly expressed view. “But those beautifully packaged, mega-budget super-flops in the film industry—are we even allowed to criticise them?…Absolutely not. That’s why they aren’t even as good as ‘Niu Lai’.”

Discomfiting though such commentary must be for officials, the phenomenon may have upsides for the government. Some netizens have poached the cartoon’s imagery to produce mini-videos suggesting that a bull run in the stock market is on its way. Officials love to promote optimism about the country’s faltering economy. Amid the bull craze, censors are standing back. ■

Subscribers can sign up to Drum Tower, our new weekly newsletter, to understand what the world makes of China—and what China makes of the world.

item.title: Chinese women are falling behind in the office
item.description:
China

China | Chaguan For those unaccustomed to truth in advertising, employers in China can be astonishingly forthright in their help-wanted notices. Huangshi, a city in Hubei, recently sought investment-promotion officers under 35 years old, specifying “men preferred”. A high-speed rail operator in...
item.content:encoded:
Chinese women are falling behind in the office

China | Chaguan


For those unaccustomed to truth in advertising, employers in China can be astonishingly forthright in their help-wanted notices. Huangshi, a city in Hubei, recently sought investment-promotion officers under 35 years old, specifying “men preferred”. A high-speed rail operator in Lanzhou wanted women, but only so long as they were under 25, over 160cm tall and with a “good appearance”. A Suzhou packaging firm, by contrast, stretched to the geriatric reaches of 45 in its search for a sales representative, adding that female candidates should already be married with children—in other words, please no maternity leave.

These are just a few blatant examples of discrimination that women face in the Chinese labour market. More extensive discrimination is largely out of sight. It includes pressure on women to avoid pregnancy, higher pay for male colleagues and fewer opportunities as women’s careers progress.

In the 1950s, when Mao Zedong declared that “women held up half the sky”, in narrowly economic terms China looked egalitarian. Men and women had similar jobs as well as incomes, though both were miserable—and that was if you were lucky enough to escape becoming victims of Mao’s revolution-without-end. Today women in China more than match men in educational terms: 51% of university students are female, up by 14 percentage points since 1995. The picture at work, by contrast, has grown worse. Men on average now earn roughly a third more. In 1990 nearly 80% of women aged between 15 and 64 were in the labour force, one of the highest rates anywhere in the world. Today that has slipped to under 70%, below both Japan and the European Union. China’s business leadership is overwhelmingly male. Women are even rarer at the top of politics. For a quarter-century until 2022, the Politburo, the Communist Party’s top body, boasted a woman or two. Since then there have been none.

Sexism is part of the problem. For businessmen and officials, the banqueting table is often where deals get done. But long boozy dinners (officially forbidden under Xi Jinping) can be offputting to women, or worse. A senior cadre and a property executive in Hangzhou, a wealthy east-central city, were recently accused of assaulting a young female employee after such a dinner. The incident provoked public outrage, including renewed calls to clean up the practice of banquets. A more common experience for women is less aggressive, though still demeaning. “Our bosses wouldn’t say it directly but they hope we act as decoration,” says Ms Dou, who worked in tech. Yet nothing is straightforward. Erica, a woman in her 20s in the events industry, says she has had more friction with female bosses than male ones. “We’re a patriarchal society, so when women break through and get power, they tend to be more controlling,” she says.

The more pervasive problem is less that of outright sexism and more how women’s role, or potential role, as mothers clashes with work. A “motherhood penalty” is common nearly everywhere. But in China the penalty is especially high, owing to a fierce work culture, an outdated retirement system and an intensifying state-led fertility push colliding with entrenched career patterns.

Compared with other countries at its level of development, China has generous maternity leave: mothers can get about half a year off work, on full pay. But the state covers only part of the salary on leave, with employers paying for the bulk. Five women in their 30s and 40s told Chaguan that their bosses expected to be informed should they be trying to get pregnant. “Speaking as a former manager, I myself wasn’t all that willing to hire women under 35,” said Ms Chen, who used to work in media. “What if she comes in and gets pregnant right away?” The government’s recent push for two-child families, aimed at reversing a fast-declining fertility rate, adds to employers’ concerns that married women are liable to take extended breaks from work.

After pregnancy, women face other hurdles. A common expectation that they will guide their children through school is hardly compatible with the long hours expected in many Chinese jobs. “Men the same age as me are in a better position,” says Ms Dou, in her early 40s. “There’s an assumption that they don’t have as much responsibility at home.” Job ads often state that candidates should be able to tolerate high stress, regularly work overtime and always be reachable. Such requirements do not discriminate specifically against women, but are deterrents to any parent with their hands full with young children—usually the mother.

Nor is there much runway left for a woman returning to work, perhaps in her early 40s. In white-collar jobs the official retirement age is just a few months over 55 for women and 60 for men (by 2040 these will be raised gradually to 58 and 63, respectively). Companies have less incentive to invest in mid-career women who have taken time off for children. “The job market is already biased enough against women,” says Ms Wu, a former web designer who left to have a child. “After 35 it is like frost on top of snow.” She is taking matters into her own hands, retraining as a drone pilot.

Policy tweaks would help, including making maternity and paternity leave more equal (many places give fathers 15 days, if they take any). More state funding for paid leave would ease the financial strain on companies. Men and women should also have the same (higher) retirement ages.

Yet what women are up against is less skewed policy than powerful social norms, especially the weight placed upon mothers. Until that changes, China is undermining its own potential. In educational terms, Chinese women already hold up more than half the sky today. In the world of work, they are getting just about a third of it. ■

item.content:encoded:
唐纳德·特朗普终于开始修建他的边境墙了

美国 | 力不从心 在亚利桑那州圣拉斐尔谷的土路和牲畜围栏上方，焊工们正在忙碌。一名工人将扁平的钢板焊接到充满混凝土的横梁上，火花四溅。最终，两堵各高30英尺（9米）且并行的墙体将横跨这片偏远的草原，将亚利桑那州与墨西哥的索诺拉州分开。唐纳德·特朗普在2015年宣布参选总统的演讲中承诺：“我将建造一堵巨大、巨大的墙。”十多年后，圣拉斐尔谷的这道屏障只是白宫计划沿美墨边境修建的“智能墙”的一部分。自州际公路系统以来，联邦政府还从未启动过如此规模的建设项目。这堵墙不止一个用途，也将产生广泛影响。对特朗普的基本盘来说，它有助于兑现竞选承诺；对政府承包商来说，它提供了机会；对潜在移民来说，它是特朗普驱逐令的永恒象征。这堵墙将改变美墨边境的性质，以及居住在边境附近的社区。然而，这堵墙宣称的目标是终结非法移民，而在这方面它的影响将十分有限。美国与墨西哥的边境绵延近2000英里（3219公里）。长期以来，那些试图遏制越境移民的人面临一个基本问题：当他们加强广袤边境某一部分的执法时，移民只会绕道而行。但自2010年代以来，移民主要不是对执法力度的变化做出反应，而是对更广泛政策的变化做出反应，尤其是庇护政策。移民们认定，他们应该向边境巡逻队自首，而不是试图逃跑；在乔·拜登总统任期内，由于更宽容的立场，这种做法激增。负责保卫美国边境的机构——海关与边境保护局（CBP）记录到，2023年12月南部边境发生了超过30万起移民遭遇事件。在拜登任期即将结束时，他姗姗来迟地限制了庇护，移民与边境巡逻队的遭遇数量开始急剧下降。在特朗普的第二任期内，这一数字又下降了79%。总统几乎完全终止了庇护，其激进的拘留和遣返行动起到了威慑作用。CBP正在庆祝胜利。图森地区（涵盖亚利桑那州数百英里）的边境巡逻队队长约翰·莫里斯表示，走私者已不再能够“一次运送50、100或300人”。“现在都是一个两个地来。”然而，总统仍然热衷于修建他的墙，以建立一道能够抵御其继任者任何政策松动的屏障。一些墙已经存在（见地图）。自乔治·H·W·布什以来的每一位总统都修建过边境屏障，包括民主党人。在亚利桑那州科奇斯县，一堵乔治·W·布什执政期间修建的带蛇腹形铁丝网的锈色18英尺高墙，与一堵30英尺高的钢墙相连，后者是特朗普第一任期修建的450英里屏障的一部分，大部分用于替换现有屏障。 边境也已经配备了技术设备。科奇斯县警长办公室运营着约1300台摄像机，可拍摄潜在移民（有时还有徒步旅行者）的图像。传感器在人们靠近边境时向CBP发出警报。当本报记者与托霍诺奥哈姆民族（一个印第安人保留地）主席弗隆·何塞一起探访边境时，探员们开着卡车出现。墨西哥军方也很快抵达了边境的另一侧。一名持枪士兵查看了现场，然后判定这群人不构成威胁。然而，没有任何一届政府尝试过建造如此规模和精密程度的边境墙。《一项大而美的法案》——国会去年通过，政府官员亲切地称其为“OB3”——拨款470亿美元用于修建屏障、通道和技术设施。OB3另有200亿美元允许CBP扩充人员并购买新装备。当特朗普开始第二任期时，南部边境已有近650英里长的墙蜿蜒分布。如今，覆盖边境超过三分之二的新屏障合同已经授出。他计划再封堵600多英里的裸露地带，并升级或补充现有屏障路段。为了配合钢梁栅栏，橙色浮标加上水下网将阻止移民试图游过格兰德河。车辆屏障、传感器、摄像头和监控塔将填补所有空隙。建墙资金必须在2029年10月之前用完，但白宫希望在特朗普离任前尽可能多地建造。在5月于菲尼克斯举行的边境安全博览会上，官员们解释了他们的支出策略。“我们正在提前投入，”直到最近还在国土安全部（DHS，CBP的上级机构）负责该法案资金拨付的杰奎琳·鲁比诺说，“到本财年九月底，我们将至少承担75%甚至更多的已拨付资金。”这引发了对合同的疯狂竞标。在菲尼克斯，销售代表们推销战术装备、无人机，以及伪装成岩石以给摄像头和传感器供电的太阳能电池板。这股热潮有少数明显的赢家。在本财年CBP授予的约220亿美元建墙合同中，近65%流向了仅仅两家公司：费舍尔砂石公司和巴纳德建筑公司。他们的老板此前曾向特朗普或其他共和党人捐款。然而，尚不清楚这堵墙是否会成为特朗普想要的永久威慑。尽管建设如火如荼，但在他离任时可能仍未完工。CBP表示计划在2028年完成建设，但截至8月19日，计划新墙仅建成了11%。8月，推土机开进了得克萨斯州的大弯国家公园，那里格兰德河切穿高耸的峡谷。重型机械撕裂公园的景象激怒了当地居民，无论是民主党人还是共和党人，他们的游说使CBP暂时停工。即使这堵墙完全按计划建好，庇护政策如果再次放松，也会通过鼓励移民在合法入境点自首，为他们提供进入美国的途径。而且，最渴望进入美国的移民总会找到办法。科奇斯县副警长杰西·米切尔解释说，走私者已经使用切割炬切开墙的钢梁，用大锤敲掉混凝土。“他们试图切得很光滑，这样探员在巡逻时就不会发现，他们就能继续把人送过来。”CBP已经警告说，承担大部分跨境人口和毒品走私的卡特尔将尝试隧道、无人机和海上路线。这些尝试可能会促使未来的政客引入新的威慑措施。2011年，巴拉克·奥巴马当时在边境沿线进行规模较小的建设投资，他预测共和党人总会要求加强防御。“现在他们会说我们需要把边境巡逻队增加四倍，”他在得克萨斯州埃尔帕索对人群说，“也许他们需要一条护城河。也许他们想让护城河里有鳄鱼。”与此同时，边境社区正准备迎接变化。尽管大弯国家公园的工程被推迟，但即使在很少有人越境的崎岖地区，建设也在进行中。“如果你想从这边过来，你将承受亚利桑那的严酷环境，”米切尔在圣拉斐尔谷说，“这里的每样东西都会咬你、刺你或扎你。”对人类来说危险的地方，对野生动物却是宝地。环保组织生物多样性中心起诉政府试图阻止建设，但被几十年前授权的豁免权所阻碍，该豁免权允许政府甚至在美洲虎和虎猫等濒危物种的栖息地建造。“这里是亚利桑那南部的生物瑰宝，”该组织的倡导者拉斯·麦克帕登哀叹道。托霍诺奥哈姆民族也起诉要求停止建墙，理由是建墙将侵犯部落主权。该民族被1854年的加兹登购地所分割，那次购地划定了美国和墨西哥之间的现代边界。新的墙将把约2000名在墨西哥的部落成员与美国成员分开。“我们没有跨越边境，是边境跨越了我们，”部落主席何塞说。一名联邦法官拒绝阻止施工，8月25日，建墙承包商开始工作。随着建设继续，边境巡逻队仍处于高度戒备状态。麦克帕登经常遇到在圣拉斐尔谷草原上巡逻的探员。最近一个傍晚，他看到一名警官站在卡车车顶上，盯着墙方向的什么东西。麦克帕登更愿意带着惊奇而不是警惕来看待这片风景。“我倒愿意相信他们只是在看月亮。”■

item.title: 从战舰到弹射器，特朗普不断折腾海军

United States

item.content:encoded:
从战舰到弹射器，特朗普不断折腾海军

美国 | 全速倒车 从乔治·华盛顿到富兰克林·罗斯福，历任总统都曾扩充美国海军，但很少有美国领导人像唐纳德·特朗普那样对舰船设计抱有如此浓厚的兴趣。他酷爱《海上胜利》（Victory at Sea），一部20世纪50年代关于美国海军在第二次世界大战中丰功伟绩的纪录片，片中战列舰发射巨炮，飞机从颠簸起伏的航空母舰甲板上起飞。在2024年共和党全国代表大会上的演讲中——那是他总统竞选中最重要的一次演讲——他脱离讲稿，吹嘘自己在第一任期内重新设计了军舰的舰艏，使其“看起来像游艇”。他声称，造船厂的反应是“这家伙似乎懂行”。这有待商榷。海军存在舰船短缺的问题，尽管国会要求拥有355艘舰船，但目前可用的不到300艘。中国拥有超过370艘。于是特朗普采取了行动。去年12月，他下令建造超大型的新“特朗普级”舰船，配备导弹发射器、激光武器和电磁轨道炮。这一设计可能并不明智——特朗普新“黄金舰队”中每艘战列舰的庞大体积，可能比拥有更多数量的小型舰艇风险更高。但他最新的要求——用过时的蒸汽弹射器取代新型航空母舰上的电磁弹射器——则绝对是倒退。弹射器是飞机从航母短飞行甲板上起飞的方式。8月13日，特朗普命令五角大楼在60天内提交一份蒸汽弹射器方案。他认为电磁弹射系统EMALS过于复杂。该系统曾出现初期问题，但似乎已经稳定下来。杰拉尔德·R·福特号航母结束了长达326天的部署，在委内瑞拉和伊朗附近海域行动，成功完成了12,000次弹射起飞。哈德逊研究所智库的布莱恩·克拉克认为，EMALS使出击率比蒸汽弹射器高出20%。它提供更平滑的加速度，减少对飞机的应力，并且可以在没有蒸汽活塞冲击的情况下发射轻型无人机。中国和法国正在为其新航母配备电磁弹射器。在特朗普看来，福特级第四艘舰船、正在建造中的多丽丝·米勒号应成为第一艘回归蒸汽弹射的舰船。这将需要重新设计，从发动机舱到弹射器铺设新的管道，并重新布置内部空间。如果舰船的重量和平衡发生变化——尤其是如果特朗普坚持移动甲板上容纳指挥所的“舰岛”——则需要进一步重新设计。为电力而优化的核动力装置，如果必须产生更多蒸汽，可能无法维持同样长的寿命。克拉克估计，仅重新设计一项的费用就高达数亿美元，而实际改装可能会给多丽丝·米勒号150亿美元的成本再增加数十亿美元。海军上将们目前保持沉默，或许希望拖延进程直到特朗普离任。正如特朗普一贯的行事风格，他的做法中既有合理之处也有怪异之处。他的备忘录允许外国公司在美国造船厂投资并最终将生产转移到美国后，为美国建造军舰。备忘录正确地指出，海军项目饱受“过度复杂的设计”之苦，并指示五角大楼采用“经过验证、可靠且负担得起的技术”。然而，EMALS如今已是经过验证的技术，而蒸汽弹射将延续不断重新设计舰船的坏习惯。最重要的是，新舰船需要更长时间才能投入使用，从而在旧舰退役时形成缺口。伊朗战争凸显了浮动空军基地的价值。但舰队已经捉襟见肘。亚伯拉罕·林肯号在海上航行超过270天后从中东返航，期间有报道称出现食品短缺和自杀未遂事件。接替它的将是此前驻扎在日本的乔治·华盛顿号，这将在对中国实力感到不安之际，使西太平洋没有航母可用。传统上，重新设计一艘舰船的收益必须超过使其退出行动的成本。这位“总建造师”似乎有着不同的考量。■ 通过《美国简报》了解美国政治最新动态，这是我们每日发送的新闻简报，快速分析最重要的政治新闻；还有《制衡》周刊，审视美国民主状况以及对选民至关重要的问题。

item.title: 唐纳德·特朗普应因制造业复苏而受到称赞吗？
item.description:
United States

美国 | 再次制造美国货 在2024年的竞选活动中，唐纳德·特朗普承诺通过关税推动美国工业城镇的复兴。在宾夕法尼亚州的拉特罗布，他发誓要“带回我们的制造业工作岗位、能源工作岗位……以及我们的梦想”。在底特律，他谈到了制造业工作岗位从墨西哥迁回密歇根。这一承诺不仅仅是更多美国制造的商品，而是更多美国人去制造它们。总统兑现了吗？ 特朗普先生相信他做到了，而且有一定道理。供应管理协会对制造业采购经理的调查显示，今年每个月工厂活动都在扩张（见图表）。美联储的工业生产指数显示，2026年上半年实际制造业产出按年化计算增长4.5%——这是自2011年以来最快的增速，不包括新冠疫情后的反弹。本月，福特表...
item.content:encoded:
唐纳德·特朗普应因制造业复苏而受到称赞吗？

美国 | 再次制造美国货 在2024年的竞选活动中，唐纳德·特朗普承诺通过关税推动美国工业城镇的复兴。在宾夕法尼亚州的拉特罗布，他发誓要“带回我们的制造业工作岗位、能源工作岗位……以及我们的梦想”。在底特律，他谈到了制造业工作岗位从墨西哥迁回密歇根。这一承诺不仅仅是更多美国制造的商品，而是更多美国人去制造它们。总统兑现了吗？ 特朗普先生相信他做到了，而且有一定道理。供应管理协会对制造业采购经理的调查显示，今年每个月工厂活动都在扩张（见图表）。美联储的工业生产指数显示，2026年上半年实际制造业产出按年化计算增长4.5%——这是自2011年以来最快的增速，不包括新冠疫情后的反弹。本月，福特表示将从2030年开始将部分车型的生产从中国转移到美国，其老板将这一决定与关税联系起来。如果说有什么行业体现了美国制造业，那就是汽车制造。特朗普先生将其作为关税政策的重点，对进口汽车和许多进口零部件征收25%的关税。美国与加拿大之间的贸易谈判最近破裂，部分原因就在于该行业。随后，特朗普先生威胁要从1月1日起将对来自加拿大的所有汽车、卡车和零部件的关税提高到50%。总统可以指出一些成果。从2025年12月到2026年7月，汽车产量跃升约9%，占制造业整体增长的约四分之一。福特并不是唯一改变计划的车企。通用汽车也将把部分生产从中国转移到美国，以避免对中国制造的汽车征收超过50%的关税。通用汽车还削减了在加拿大的业务。Stellantis（其最大股东部分拥有《经济学人》的母公司）已将未来生产从加拿大转移到美国。本田正将思域的生产从墨西哥迁至印第安纳州。然而，这些计划并不能很好地解释已经发生的产出反弹。这更多归因于去年年底供应中断后的恢复、对皮卡和SUV的强劲需求，以及新车型的推出。目前，关税更多的是推高成本而非提振产出。通用汽车估计，关税今年将使其损失25亿至35亿美元，主要原因是它仍进口整车和零部件。在其他行业，上涨趋势在特朗普先生重返白宫之前就已在进行中。今年上半年飞机产量增长近9%，但该行业的复苏始于2022年。电气设备制造商仍在受益于乔·拜登领导下政策加速的投资周期。国家电气制造商协会的唐纳德·莱文斯表示，对可再生能源的补贴帮助刺激了变压器工厂和其他电网设备的支出。“其中很多影响今天仍在显现。”一些最强劲的制造业部门也是受关税保护最少的部门。以人工智能热潮为例，它通过数据中心和能源基础设施的建设提升了设备和材料的需求。从2025年12月到2026年7月，半导体和电子元件的产出增长了超过12%，数据中心冷却设备增长了近4%，水泥增长了近9%。《经济学人》估计，2026年上半年，数据中心和电力建设占制造业产出增长的近三分之一。虽然一些人工智能硬件（如芯片）日益成为关税政策的目标，但许多与人工智能相关的进口已被排除在更广泛的关税之外。这种模式超出了人工智能领域。自由意志主义智库卡托研究所的斯科特·林西科姆计算得出，航空航天、计算机和电子产品的有效关税税率低于5%，属于制造业中最低的。与此同时，面临更高关税的制造业主力——从食品到纺织品——今年几乎没有增长。对选民来说，特朗普政策真正的考验是就业。在这一点上，复兴更难找到。今年前七个月，制造业就业人数仅增加约31,000人——与2023年至2025年间失去的315,000个工厂工作岗位相比，增幅微乎其微。航空航天和与人工智能相关建设相关的行业贡献了所有净就业增长。与此同时，在更传统的制造业中，就业人数下降。即使在一些推动产出反弹的行业中，就业增长也有限。汽车行业就业人数增长不到1%。芯片制造商在产出激增的同时却裁员。在制造业工作岗位出现的地方，它们看起来与特朗普先生所唤起的那种传统工厂工作不同。例如，飞机工厂需要工程师和技术人员。近六成工人拥有学士或更高学位；只有五分之一的人在工厂车间工作。基础设施繁荣也同样需要高智商。换句话说，这场复兴明显缺乏工厂工人。即使本十年晚些时候有更多汽车制造回流，大量的装配工人也不会回来。机器人现在承担了大部分工作。与此同时，扩张最快的行业正在努力寻找足够的熟练工人。特朗普先生的总统任期可能会带来自动化工厂的投资，并创造对高端人才的需求。这将构成制造业复兴，但也许不是他的支持者们所希望的那种。■ 通过《The US in brief》（我们的每日通讯，快速分析最重要的政治新闻）和《Checks and Balance》（一份每周简报，审视美国民主状况和对选民重要的问题），随时了解美国政治。

item.title: Shrimpers are the latest group seeking protection from Washington
item.description:
United States

United States | Pro-tariff crustaceans “WE SHOULD BE excited, but we’re not because we got a boatload of shrimp and it’s worth no money,” says Waylon Buras, watching his men unload a 40,000-pound haul onto the docks of the Louisiana bayou. The fisherman had just returned home after 13 days at s...
item.content:encoded:
Shrimpers are the latest group seeking protection from Washington

United States | Pro-tariff crustaceans


“WE SHOULD BE excited, but we’re not because we got a boatload of shrimp and it’s worth no money,” says Waylon Buras, watching his men unload a 40,000-pound haul onto the docks of the Louisiana bayou. The fisherman had just returned home after 13 days at sea, the longest trip of his career. Lifting a fistful of iridescent shrimp to the sun, he notes with frustration how perfect they are: “They look like glass.” In May a pound sold for $2.00, but today he will get just $1.80.

Cheap shrimp from abroad keep driving down prices, while high fuel costs wipe away any remaining profit. He wants the government to do more. “They can either subsidise us at the end of the year or they need to put a hold on the imports so we can catch our breath,” he says. “We’re almost drowning.”

Gulf-coast shrimpers from Alabama to Texas are the latest group hoping to benefit from Donald Trump’s tariffs. Last year taxes on imported food more than quadrupled. Mr Trump has not stopped imports of shrimp, but in July his trade representative announced duties of at least 10% on a broad swathe of goods, including shrimp from countries such as Vietnam and Indonesia. The problem for shrimpers, as for some other American industries, is that tariffs may not be enough to save them, and may in the meantime raise costs for everyone else.

American shrimpers didn’t always struggle to compete. When seafood casseroles and Jell-O salads became popular in the mid-20th century, housewives bought home-grown shrimp. Then aid programmes scrambled the economics. In the 1970s, the World Bank and USAID spent billions teaching malnourished communities in Latin America and South-East Asia how to fish at scale.

Today nearly 95% of the shrimp Americans eat is imported; in four decades the share harvested in the Gulf fell from 29% to 4.5%. A National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) report published in March found that a pandemic-era glut turned a simmering problem into a crisis. Between 2021 and 2023 prices of Gulf shrimp halved, making shrimping unprofitable. Crews stopped going out to sea and the industry lost 1,200 jobs. Revenue more than halved in just two years, to $221m. Hurricanes and oil spills add more risk. “Every shock shrinks the fleet,” says Christopher Liese, an economist at NOAA who wrote the recent report.

The shrimp lobby was relieved to be included in the administration’s tariff announcement in July. Jessica Domangue, a representative in the Louisiana House, reckons big-shots in Washington are finally “waking up” to the plight of her constituents. However it is unclear how long the tariffs will last.

Twenty-five states have sued to block Mr Trump’s new levies, which the White House has sought to impose under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act. If they are held to be legal, Mr Trump may himself move to lower them. The president seems to be realising that tariffs do indeed raise prices and that American consumers don’t like that; voters now rank affordability as their top concern. Florida lobbyists persuaded the White House to place a heavy duty on Mexican tomatoes, which supply 70% of the domestic market. In the nine months to April, tomato prices surged by 50%. Such effects were predictable. In the 1930s sugar magnates secured the dream protection package: tariffs, production caps and price supports from the government. Americans now pay a fifth more than the global average for sugar. The American Enterprise Institute, a think-tank, estimates that the policies cost each household $40 a year and keep just 4,000 farms afloat.

For some food products, Mr Trump is now reversing course. After raising fees on coffee, cocoa, beef, bananas and avocados last summer, the administration lowered them a few months later (see chart). Facing a broad backlash over grocery prices, on August 21st the president said he would let 300,000 tonnes of ground beef be imported, tariff-free, for 90 days. Hamburger-lovers cheered; cattle ranchers are furious. Pete Ricketts, a Republican senator from Nebraska being challenged by a left-leaning Independent, Dan Osborn, was among the president’s usual allies to break rank. “Flooding the market with lower-quality beef”, Mr Ricketts wrote on X, “compromises Nebraska farmers and ranchers.”

Even if tariffs do remain, they are unlikely to solve the economics of shrimping. “Tariffs may buy time but won’t make the industry competitive or make the underlying issues go away,” says David Ortega, a food economist at Michigan State University. The average vessel in the fleet that fishes federal waters in the Gulf is 34 years old. Chronic problems have made reinvesting in infrastructure a bad bet. Some legislators are now pushing for more changes. Bills in Congress would bar federal funds from supporting overseas aquaculture and require the government to buy only American shrimp for school lunches, military cafeterias and food programmes.

Back on the bayou it is clear how much has been lost since the glory days of American shrimping. Years ago fishermen would fill the pool hall after a hard day’s work and there were dances in a community ballroom every weekend. Now abandoned packing sheds dot the coastline. Some residents have taken to meth and the Family Dollar store closed a few months ago.

Mr Buras reckons things are getting worse. Before this trip, his crew asked for a little extra money upfront to buy clothes for their children for the new school year. In the boat’s cramped air-conditioned quarters, as shrimp are vacuumed out from its underbelly, the men explain why they keep at it. “It’s an addiction,” says Mr Buras’s son-in-law. They like the freedom, they say, and the sunsets. In four days they go back out to sea.■

Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

item.content:encoded:
可能塑造民主党获胜信息的州

美国 | 列克星敦 在这个夏日将尽、民主党乐观情绪渐涨的日子里——党内越来越希望重新夺回华盛顿的部分权力，并开始摆脱在国民心中精英主义和无能的形象——没有哪个州比俄亥俄州更具可能性。俄亥俄曾是美国政治的晴雨表，但本世纪以来，随着民主党失去工人阶级选民的支持，该州已稳固地倒向共和党。但民调显示，民主党不仅有机会赢下参议院席位，还有可能赢得州长职位——自1991年以来，他们仅在该职位上成功执政过一届。他们甚至可能赢得一两个众议院席位。高油价、关税以及唐纳德·特朗普的极度不受欢迎，正在提高民主党在中西部的胜算。在俄亥俄州，公众对数据中心的态度急转直下，对在该州占据主导地位的共和党来说尤为棘手。参议员乔恩·赫斯特德正面临前民主党参议员谢罗德·布朗的挑战，他匆忙提出一项法案，以保护消费者免受数据中心导致的电费上涨之苦。但他此前曾为这些数据中心的建设欢呼。全国共和党参议员委员会本月致信人工智能公司，寻求帮助以抵御布朗等人的攻击，警告数据中心已成为“挂在赫斯特德脖子上的锚”。阿克伦大学政治学家戴维·科恩将共和党人试图摆脱与数据中心共谋关系的做法，比作银行劫匪打开赃款袋却突然被里面的染料包炸了一脸。“那些染料可不会消失，”他说。他认为民主党可能横扫全州性职位并赢下参议院席位。“我是说，你能感觉到，”他说，“一场政治地震即将发生。”

俄亥俄州的民主党人避免了密歇根州和威斯康星州等中西部州那种进步派与温和派之间的自相残杀。俄亥俄的民主党人看起来像是另一个时代的政党成员：他们不纠结于文化议题和以色列问题，而是聚焦于民生经济议题——降低医疗成本、提高工资、加强公共教育、保护消费者和有组织劳工。“这在俄亥俄已经是最主流的做法了，”约翰·库莱维奇说。他正竞选成为16年来首位民主党州检察长。因此，如果这些民主党信息通过实地检验，它们可能为2028年的全国候选人提供一套具有广泛吸引力的纲领。

在俄亥俄州，真正登上头条的是共和党内部一种特别恶劣的内斗。代表第七选区的两届众议员马克斯·米勒被前妻艾米丽·莫雷诺指控虐待她和她两岁的女儿。他否认了这些指控，并指责她伤害了他们的孩子。警方和儿童福利机构历时数月的调查发现，虐待行为“确有迹象”，但未能确定施暴者。父母继续共同享有监护权。莫雷诺女士是共和党参议员伯尼·莫雷诺的女儿，后者在2024年击败了布朗。莫雷诺本月表示，米勒在获得“严肃的心理帮助”之前，“不应继续自由地危害他人”。米勒此前指责莫雷诺参与“他女儿那场毁掉我人生的恶意运动”。他已以诽谤罪起诉莫雷诺女士。这场法律斗争揭开了竞选的一角：在法庭文件中，米勒表示莫雷诺的指控让他失去了背书和捐款，并可能使他的竞选成本翻倍。在他为自己的席位而战时，他将自己的坚持描绘成一种与特朗普相似的坚韧——他曾是特朗普第一任期内的助手。然而，一个表明选民关切可能有利于合适类型民主党人的迹象是，米勒还在宣扬他“投票保护奥巴马医改”的记录。

这场竞选中令人惊讶的一点——最不引人注意的一点——是，直到这场轩然大波出现，全国民主党才对手竞争的对手布莱恩·波因德克斯特表现出多少兴趣。虽然该选区倾向于共和党，但库克政治报告认为其共和党优势仅为五个百分点，如果蓝色浪潮正在形成，这是一个可以跨越的障碍。更令人费解的是，波因德克斯特正是民主党急于塑造形象的完美候选人：他是工会成员的儿子和孙子，15岁就到机械车间工作，已经当了19年钢铁工人。在8月25日向伊利里亚市罢工的县政府雇员发表讲话之前接受采访时，波因德克斯特坚称民主党“一直支持工薪家庭”。但他表示，因为民主党“上了共和党人的当”，开始强调文化议题，才失去了工薪阶层的支持。尽管伯尼·桑德斯为他背书，但波因德克斯特对全套左翼议程持保留态度。他不想废除移民与海关执法局，也不急于实施全民医保。除了亲工会的立场，他的议程相当模糊。他不加修饰的演讲、褪色的蓝色牛仔裤和总是横别在腰带上的手机，让他完全依靠自己的经历以及与米勒——出身于克利夫兰最富有家族之一的人——的对比。“我就是人们在政治中渴望已久的东西——一个和他们一模一样的人，”波因德克斯特说。他的背景使他更适合阶级政治，而非激烈的党派政治，这也像老一代俄亥俄民主党人。2008年，波因德克斯特投票支持共和党参议员约翰·麦凯恩竞选总统，2012年则投票给巴拉克·奥巴马，他对两人都极为钦佩。在竞选活动中，他谈到父亲对特朗普的支持，以及他多么敬爱父亲。“各位，我们分歧之间的某个地方藏着正确答案，”他8月15日在梅迪纳对选民说。这可能是今年从俄亥俄州传出的最激进的信息。■

item.title: The costs of defying Donald Trump are mounting for Canada
item.description:
The Americas

The Americas | Deal or no deal Mark Carney is governing through paradox. Canada’s largest trading partner, the United States, is led by an unreliable man who uses trade barriers as a weapon. For Canada, the diversification of trade partners is wise, but takes time. Building infrastructure neede...
item.content:encoded:
The costs of defying Donald Trump are mounting for Canada

The Americas | Deal or no deal


Mark Carney is governing through paradox. Canada’s largest trading partner, the United States, is led by an unreliable man who uses trade barriers as a weapon. For Canada, the diversification of trade partners is wise, but takes time. Building infrastructure needed to serve new markets requires significant investment. And yet little would do more to get that investment flowing than a trade deal with the United States.

The pursuit of such a deal has pushed both countries to the brink of a full-blown trade war. Minutes before midnight on August 21st, two days after Donald Trump said that “a very good deal for both parties” was all but done, Canada’s prime minister abandoned the talks, allowing fresh tariffs of up to 50% to come into force on 5% of Canadian exports to the United States, worth $20bn. Mr Trump’s price for normal trade relations was too high. “Our goal has been to secure the best deal for Canadians,” Mr Carney said on August 22nd. “Never a deal at any price.”

And so on August 25th Canada matched the new American tariffs with levies of its own on some $20bn of American exports, with implementation delayed until September 8th. Support for Mr Carney’s decision to walk away is widespread in Canada. A survey by the Angus Reid Institute, a pollster, suggests that 76% of Canadians back the move. The political risk that comes with signing a trade deal Canadians cannot stomach is far higher than that from Mr Trump’s tariffs.

But however bad Mr Trump’s deal might have been for Canada in the long run, declining it and letting new tariffs come into force will start to hurt soon. The Canadian economy grew by 0.8% between the first and second quarters of this year, having grown by just 1.7% in 2025 after the first round of tariffs came into force in March that year. Unemployment hit a two-year low of 6.4% in July, but inflation is creeping up. David Colletto, the boss of Abacus Data, a pollster, points out that almost two-thirds of Canadian voters cite the cost of living as their most important issue. Nothing else comes close. “The threat”, says Mr Colletto, “is not that Canadians tire of the fight. It is that the fight collides with the cost of living.”

That seems unavoidable. Trevor Tombe, an economist at the University of Calgary, estimates that Mr Trump’s new tariffs will push inflation to 4%. Some 90,000 Canadians could lose their jobs, bringing the unemployment rate up to 7%. And that does not account for damage that will be caused by the retaliatory tariffs.

If Mr Carney follows through on September 8th, retaliation will come with domestic political risks as much as economic ones. Some provincial premiers, such as Doug Ford in Ontario, are gung-ho; in July Mr Ford said that Canada could “dismantle the US if we wanted to” by cutting off energy supplies. But others, particularly Danielle Smith, the premier of Alberta, are much quieter. Alberta provides the United States with about half of its imported oil and has been almost entirely spared from Mr Trump’s duties so far.

Mr Carney has previously ruled out weaponising Canada’s energy exports, perhaps in part because doing so might irritate Ms Smith’s constituents. He is now being urged, at a minimum, to consider the possibility of applying an export duty on Canadian energy bound for the United States if Mr Trump follows through on his fresh threat to double tariffs on Canadian-built automobiles to 50%. “I don’t think they want us to stop sending any of that energy,” Mr Carney said on August 22nd.

Any levy on Canadian energy is fraught with peril. Large eastern cities such as Toronto and Montreal get much of their fuel via pipelines that run through the United States, carrying hydrocarbons both from Alberta and American sources. On August 24th Mr Trump made a veiled threat to turn off the tap.

The more existential danger would be to Canada’s national unity. In October Albertans will vote in a referendum (triggered by a petition) which asks whether they are happy to remain in Canada or would prefer to hold a second and binding referendum on secession. Even if Mr Ford is right that energy exports give Canada leverage over the United States, it is not a weapon that can be used without risking great self-harm. The effect of Canada’s federal government cutting off rich Albertans from their biggest customer is hard to predict, but it is unlikely to help the argument for the province to remain Canadian.

Provincial politics also explain part of Mr Carney’s motivation for declining Mr Trump’s deal. Quebecers will vote in October for a new provincial government. Public-opinion surveys suggest the separatist Parti Québécois holds a slim lead. Mr Carney says the United States wanted to water down measures protecting Canada’s French-language and culture, a demand that, if acquiesced to, might have empowered separatism in Quebec, too.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs target states such as Michigan and Maine where Republican senators are struggling in tight midterm races. Mr Carney must hope that America’s cost-of-living issues, inflamed by higher prices on Canadian imports, push Mr Trump to reopen talks and thereby, at last, give Canada some stability. ■

item.title: Donald Trump’s military expansion in Panama makes little sense
item.description:
The Americas

The Americas | Welcome to the jungle SPEEDBOATS INTERCEPT a suspicious ship near the entrance to the Panama Canal. Troops board it and bundle the bad guys off. On the Caribbean coast, special forces launch an assault on a rebel base. On the outskirts of Panama city, the capital, Chinook and Bla...
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s military expansion in Panama makes little sense

The Americas | Welcome to the jungle


SPEEDBOATS INTERCEPT a suspicious ship near the entrance to the Panama Canal. Troops board it and bundle the bad guys off. On the Caribbean coast, special forces launch an assault on a rebel base. On the outskirts of Panama city, the capital, Chinook and Black Hawk helicopters buzz overhead. From August 3rd to 13th, Panamanians witnessed a display of military prowess not seen in the country for almost two decades.

This was Panamax, a multinational military exercise led by the United States to practise fending off possible threats to the Panama Canal. Held roughly every two years since 2003, for the past 13 its simulation has been run from bases in Texas and Florida. This year it was done in Panama proper. Over 1,700 troops, mostly American but including soldiers from 17 (mostly Latin American) countries, engaged in “kinetic operations” across the country.

“I’ve no issue with tabletop exercises but you can’t replicate this,” said Pete Hegseth, the secretary of war, dressed in a sweat-soaked olive-green t-shirt. The canal is “a key piece of terrain. We’ve got more troops here in partnership with Panama than we’ve had in a very long time.”

The United States has renewed its interest in the western hemisphere since Donald Trump regained office. It has intervened militarily in Venezuela, ramped up economic pressure on Cuba, bullied Canada and menaced Greenland. And Mr Trump has repeatedly threatened to take control of the Panama Canal. For Southcom, the US Joint Command focused on Latin America, “ensuring unfettered US access to the Panama Canal is a top priority.” But this military expansionism does not sit comfortably with the treaties that govern the canal. And how effective will it be?

Mr Hegseth was speaking at Fort Sherman, one of three American-Panamanian training schools he announced on his previous trip, in April 2025. In the second half of the 20th century hundreds of thousands of troops undertook gruelling jungle-warfare training at Fort Sherman, many of them before being sent to Vietnam. “Green Hell” was closed in 1999, along with 13 other American military installations, as a condition of the 1977 Canal Neutrality Treaty, which banned foreign military installations. Panama’s government says the revived “Jungle School” is not a new foreign military base. But opposition politicians call it a “camouflaged invasion”.

Panama’s constitution bars the country from having an army, but since becoming president in 2024 José Raúl Mulino has beefed up Senafront, the border-control force, and Senan, the naval and air service. Last year Panama agreed to buy four Brazilian fighter planes. In April it received the first of an order of surveillance drones and interceptor boats from the United States. Together with port-scanning and cyber-security equipment, the United States has given technology worth more than $174m to the security forces, says Mr Mulino. In August his government launched a new joint command of Panamanian security forces, funded by canal revenue and dedicated to defending the waterway and its hydrographic basin.

Panamax was also a chance for Latin American members of the Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition, formerly known as the Shield of the Americas, to meet. Mr Hegseth said Colombia, along with Honduras and Guatemala, had agreed to allow joint American military operations in their territory “to bring the fight to the [designated terrorist organisations] on land”. (Guatemala denies it has agreed.)

With Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, promising an aggressive campaign against criminal groups, Panama is preparing to deal with the spillover. On August 15th Senafront sent more than 700 special forces to Panama’s southern border to try to stop gangsters entering through the heavily forested Darién Gap that separates the two countries. “The canal’s enemy is narco-trafficking, and no one else,” says Mr Mulino.

The United States disagrees. The Trump administration reckons China, not drug gangs, poses the most serious threat to the canal. It wants to drive Chinese activity away from all the critical infrastructure it can in Latin America. Last year it pushed Panama to remove Chinese operators from the ports at each end of the canal. Such “dual-use infrastructure” could be used for “intelligence gathering, cyber vulnerability, or logistical denial during global contingencies”, according to Southcom. Mr Hegseth views Panama as part of “Greater North America” and part of the “immediate security perimeter”.

“The Panama Canal is probably the most important infrastructure in the western hemisphere,” says Kevin Cabrera, America’s ambassador to Panama. “If you wanted to interrupt our commerce, the Panama Canal is the way to mess with that.” Military co-ordination is crucial to defending the waterway, he says.

But reviving Jungle School hardly tackles these concerns. American troops cannot stop spying or cyber-attacks by other states. Much bigger numbers of them would be needed to prevent drone attacks or sabotage by terrorists.

Instead, increased American meddling may increase risks to the canal. Panamanian schoolchildren are taught that their country’s neutrality is the canal’s best defence, while its openness to all vessels “in times of peace and in times of war” has boosted its role in world trade. Rodrigo Noriega, a local analyst, says Mr Trump’s mercantilism threatens this neutrality, with the result that the chances of the canal being targeted are growing. Mr Cabrera dismisses this. “State and non-state actors don’t care about the rule of law. They don’t care about treaties,” he says.

By contrast, Panama is seeking to bolster the Neutrality Treaty. Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Portugal and Switzerland have signed up. Japan, India and 12 others have been sounded out. Neutrality, Mr Noriega notes, protects Panama not just from physical attacks on its canal, but potentially from Mr Trump’s bullying too. ■

The Americas

item.content:encoded:
世界最古老木乃伊的问题

美洲 | 死寂的等待 沿阿塔卡马沙漠海岸延伸600公里，从秘鲁南部到智利北部，有一处世界上最早木乃伊的群葬地。从公元前7000年到公元前1000年，生活在海岸地带、以狩猎和捕鱼为生的钦乔罗人，是死者遗体的细致保存者。几乎所有去世的人都会被制成木乃伊，不论社会地位高低。这一点，加上阿塔卡马干燥的环境，导致了一种奇怪的局面：世界上有意保存的最古老遗体数量如此之多，以至于它们正在制造问题。近来，有更多遗骸从地下浮现。塞萨尔·博列是智利政府委托保护该国钦乔罗考古遗址的机构“钦乔罗印记”的考古学家。他正在研究一具在卡莱塔卡马罗内斯镇（位于智利北部阿里卡市附近）散步时偶然发现的骨架。“我们每次来这里都会发现新的暴露遗骸，”他一边说，一边用手轻轻地将骨头重新掩埋。“在条件合适之前让它们留在土里，是我们能做的最好的事。”这不是新现象。至少自20世纪初以来，钦乔罗木乃伊就一直在从地下冒出。1917年的初步考察将木乃伊运往智利各地的博物馆，专家们在那里保存它们以供研究。考古学家也一直进行发掘，直到1990年代。但极端风力造成的侵蚀和附近日益增多的人类活动，正在加速木乃伊的暴露。该地区已经没有空间来接收这些遗体并加以保存。博列先生说，要分发所有这些木乃伊需要数百辆卡车。“博物馆里没有地方存放这些木乃伊，而不会让它们暴露在有害的光线和温度下。”智利首都圣地亚哥自然历史博物馆的人类学家维罗妮卡·席尔瓦说。 因此，渴望更深入了解钦乔罗人历时数月的木乃伊制作仪式的考古学家，不得不就地研究这些遗体，研究完后将其重新掩埋。“在我们拥有合适的技术之前，我们更愿意把它们留在地下，而不是继续发掘。”同样来自“钦乔罗印记”机构的卡米拉·卡斯蒂略说。阿里卡南部一座正在建设的新博物馆应该会有所帮助。2021年，联合国教科文组织将钦乔罗遗骸及其景观列入世界遗产名录。这提供了一个可能的解决方案：将这些遗址开发成旅游景点，并在那里安置许多木乃伊。但并非所有人都对此感到满意。一个小型渔业社区在该遗址内的卡梅罗内斯山谷非法搭建了临时住所。联合国教科文组织希望他们搬迁，但他们并不太愿意。与此同时，他们的人数不断增加，他们的存在对遗骸的破坏也越来越大。当地市长克里斯蒂安·萨瓦拉表示，木乃伊比他的选民得到更多关注，这加剧了紧张局势。但一些年长居民，比如在该地区生活了30多年的何塞·孔查，理解这些木乃伊带来的经济机遇。“我太老了，不能再打鱼了，”他说，“我很乐意成为一名导游，向游客讲解这些木乃伊。”卡斯蒂略女士说，“钦乔罗印记”希望筹集资金设立一个中心，在那里可以与卡马罗内斯居民合作研究和展出木乃伊。但如果这要奏效，考古学家就需要表明，他们既关心卡莱塔卡马罗内斯的过去，也同样关心它的未来。■

item.title: 伊朗将能摆脱美国的金融威胁
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

中东与非洲 | 压力渐失 当唐纳德·特朗普将近六个月前发起“史诗愤怒”行动时，他希望美国的军事力量能摧毁伊朗政权。当炸弹未能奏效时，他又寄望于甜头。六月，美国向伊朗提供制裁减免和数十亿美元的投资，希望该国领导人能开放霍尔木兹海峡并放弃任何核野心。这一招也失败了。于是特朗普誓言要通过在经济上击垮伊朗来瓦解该政权。他说这项努力将是一场“经济版D日”。但当财政部长斯科特·贝森特于8月24日公布细节时，他的威胁显得空洞无力。自1979年伊斯兰革命以来，伊朗一直处于美国制裁之下。在第一个任期内，特朗普对该政权施加了他所谓的“极限施压”，以迫使其在核计划上做出让步。这项名为“经济放逐行动”的新运动，大概...
item.content:encoded:
伊朗将能摆脱美国的金融威胁

中东与非洲 | 压力渐失 当唐纳德·特朗普将近六个月前发起“史诗愤怒”行动时，他希望美国的军事力量能摧毁伊朗政权。当炸弹未能奏效时，他又寄望于甜头。六月，美国向伊朗提供制裁减免和数十亿美元的投资，希望该国领导人能开放霍尔木兹海峡并放弃任何核野心。这一招也失败了。于是特朗普誓言要通过在经济上击垮伊朗来瓦解该政权。他说这项努力将是一场“经济版D日”。但当财政部长斯科特·贝森特于8月24日公布细节时，他的威胁显得空洞无力。自1979年伊斯兰革命以来，伊朗一直处于美国制裁之下。在第一个任期内，特朗普对该政权施加了他所谓的“极限施压”，以迫使其在核计划上做出让步。这项名为“经济放逐行动”的新运动，大概是“极限施压”的加强版。除了执行对伊朗石油出口的封锁外，美国还将加大对伊朗贸易伙伴以及帮助该政权转移资金的机构的压力。但这些威胁雷声大雨点小。各国不必立即遵守美国的要求。财长承认这只是“警告性射击”。伊朗正深陷经济困境。自1月以来，里亚尔对美元汇率已下跌约三分之一。在贝森特宣布之前，里亚尔跌至历史最低点，尽管后来略有反弹。战争摧毁了伊朗工业的很大一部分。炼油厂受损导致燃料短缺，加油站排起长队。通货膨胀同比高达88%。该政权正在印钞以支付食品券。 与此同时，美国对霍尔木兹海峡的封锁导致伊朗的石油出口——该政权的主要收入来源——崩塌。8月20日，伊朗央行行长表示石油出口已“降至零”。据贸易情报公司Kpler称，伊朗在霍尔木兹海峡外的船上仍有约8000万桶石油。但这仅能提供其通常此类出口收入的一小部分。贝森特没有点名他希望哪些国家减少与伊朗的贸易。但有几个国家很突出。在美国封锁之前，中国一直以低于市场价格每桶7至12美元的价格购买伊朗石油，绕过了现有的美国禁运。去年，中国买下了伊朗约90%的原油出口，美国认为这为伊朗政权提供了近一半的预算。阿联酋对伊朗的出口额超过任何其他国家。2024年，它提供了伊朗总进口的约30%。它还设有伊朗政权用来规避制裁的影子银行。据报道，今年四月美国财政部致函阿联酋领导人，要求其关闭此类机构。美国并非唯一试图对伊朗施加经济痛苦的国家。过去几个月，阿联酋对伊朗的态度有所软化，恢复贸易并允许伊朗居民返回。但8月18日，在伊朗政权对其船只发动打击后，阿联酋表示将停止与伊朗的所有贸易和金融交易。贝森特称阿联酋是“非常好的伙伴”。但其金融体系不透明。伊朗的交易经常通过空壳公司伪装，因此尽管阿联酋实施禁令，资金仍可能继续流动。其他国家将公开抵制美国的压力。中国警告称，新制裁可能损害全球增长和金融稳定，并誓言保护其“合法权益”。美国此前曾针对参与伊朗石油贸易的中国企业；四月，美国对恒力实施制裁，美方官员指控这家炼油商购买了价值数十亿美元的伊朗原油。但美国可能不愿进一步行动，因为担心报复或破坏特朗普对华外交接触。“如果你开始针对中国企业，那就不再是伊朗问题，”伦敦智库Bourse and Bazaar的埃斯凡迪亚尔·巴特曼盖利吉认为，“那是你中国政策的问题。”即便美国对中国大型银行实施二级制裁，伊朗仍可能使用自己的支付系统与中国交易。伊朗领导人对这些威胁嗤之以鼻。议会议长穆罕默德·巴盖尔·卡利巴夫在社交媒体上嘲笑美国谈论“D日”：“这不是诺曼底。”伊朗强硬派国家安全顾问穆赫辛·雷扎伊将特朗普的经济战威胁斥为“宣传”。他不无道理地问道：“他想做什么以前没做过的事？”如果进一步的经济困难引发类似一月份爆发的那种示威，该政权将陷入麻烦。但目前来看，这似乎不太可能。伊朗已在公开处决抗议者。伊朗领导人将美国转向经济施压视为其对手无意继续失败的军事行动的证据。这可能鼓励伊朗发动新的攻击，试图从特朗普那里获得让步。雷扎伊表示，任何与美国合作的国家都将被视为“敌人”，并可能成为目标。伊朗对其邻国如伊拉克拥有相当的筹码，伊拉克购买其天然气并驻有其多个武装代理人。而且霍尔木兹海峡始终存在。在贝森特宣布前几小时，伊朗威胁要对海峡中近50艘船只处以罚款或扣押，称这些船只违反了其通行规则。该政权领导人深知其经济举步维艰。卡利巴夫已承认，没有经济增长，伊朗将“无法生存”。总统马苏德·佩泽希齐扬敦促美国回到六月提出的谅解备忘录。该备忘录设定了结束战斗的框架，并承诺让伊朗重新融入全球经济。巴特曼盖利吉表示，伊朗人不想落得朝鲜那样的境地，“因为制裁依然存在，他们继续承受巨大代价”。8月24日，一直在特朗普和伊朗之间斡旋的巴基斯坦陆军参谋长阿西姆·穆尼尔访问了德黑兰，据报道是为了讨论重启双方谈判。但即便美国真的续签谅解备忘录，这样做也解决不了导致其破裂的霍尔木兹分歧。伊朗仍有能力惩罚其对手——而且它不太可能克制自己。美国谈论扼杀伊朗经济，看起来像是为了避免又一轮战斗。它可能反而会适得其反。■

item.title: 胡塞武装如何成为伊朗最可怕的盟友
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

中东与非洲 | 阿拉伯半岛的西南战线 也门长期内战中的不稳固停火已持续四年。但现在，公开冲突再次爆发。伊朗支持的反政府胡塞武装指责也门国际承认的政府及其最重要盟友沙特阿拉伯计划发动大规模进攻。7月30日，胡塞武装领导人阿卜杜勒-马利克·胡塞表示，他的部队将“以我们自己的全面升级来回应他们的全面升级”。整个8月，他们向政府军阵地发动了无人机和导弹袭击，造成数十名士兵和平民死亡。也门正规军则予以猛烈反击。 胡塞武装认为重启战争能带来许多好处。自7月中旬以来，他们的民兵一直在红海袭击与沙特有关的船只，以及港口、机场和炼油厂。根据数据提供商Kpler的数据，本月几乎没有沙特油轮通过红海南端的曼德海...
item.content:encoded:
胡塞武装如何成为伊朗最可怕的盟友

中东与非洲 | 阿拉伯半岛的西南战线 也门长期内战中的不稳固停火已持续四年。但现在，公开冲突再次爆发。伊朗支持的反政府胡塞武装指责也门国际承认的政府及其最重要盟友沙特阿拉伯计划发动大规模进攻。7月30日，胡塞武装领导人阿卜杜勒-马利克·胡塞表示，他的部队将“以我们自己的全面升级来回应他们的全面升级”。整个8月，他们向政府军阵地发动了无人机和导弹袭击，造成数十名士兵和平民死亡。也门正规军则予以猛烈反击。 胡塞武装认为重启战争能带来许多好处。自7月中旬以来，他们的民兵一直在红海袭击与沙特有关的船只，以及港口、机场和炼油厂。根据数据提供商Kpler的数据，本月几乎没有沙特油轮通过红海南端的曼德海峡。胡塞武装的袭击有两个目标：第一，要挟沙特王国支付也门公务员工资并解除对航班和航运的限制；第二，夺取主动权。如果沙特及其盟友确实在计划进攻，胡塞武装已经先发制人。他们可能还有更大的目标。自2014年以来，胡塞武装控制了也门西北部，包括首都萨那，以及西海岸的大部分地区。约70%的也门人生活在他们的统治之下。但这些反政府武装一直想要更多。8月15日，胡塞武装的导弹击中曼德海峡附近的穆哈港，迫使该港关闭。这些袭击似乎旨在削弱由政府支持的精锐战斗力量“民族抵抗力量”，该力量以穆哈为基地。迫使他们撤离该城将使胡塞武装对海峡航运拥有更多控制权。胡塞武装还想要控制也门的油田。2022年初，他们几乎占领了萨那以东马里卜的油井，但被一支由阿联酋训练、忠于政府的民兵击退。那年晚些时候，他们轰炸了沿海的石油终端，以阻止对手出口燃料。但今年7月，政府表示将恢复石油运输。此后，胡塞武装对马里卜发动了猛烈打击。他们的战士可能再次向其资源发起进攻。即使未能占领油井，他们也可能希望通过施压迫使政府分享收入。

作为回应，政府也在宣扬战斗。四年前的停火本应促成和平协议，但胡塞武装反而巩固了权力，加强了与伊朗的伙伴关系。给他们一个教训可能有助于政府——其领导人大多居住在沙特首都利雅得——在也门重新赢得信誉。这种言论可能主要是为了提振士气。但反胡塞力量在冬季大部分时间内斗之后，正在展现更加团结的阵线。政府已解散了由阿联酋支持的分裂主义组织“南方过渡委员会”，并将其部分部队纳入国家军队控制之下。今年早些时候，胡塞武装控制的焦夫地区爆发部落骚乱，引发了人们对反政府武装权威削弱的希望。政府军在部署无人机方面也变得更加熟练，而无人机一直是胡塞武装的优势之一。尽管如此，他们仍面对可怕的对手。沙特和政府军有限度的打击未能威慑反政府武装。胡塞武装过去曾承受过更大规模、更有针对性的军事行动。去年夏天，以色列的袭击杀死了该组织大部分文职领导层，但它迅速恢复。击败胡塞武装将十分困难。2014年他们横扫萨那时，实际上是违抗了伊朗的意愿，当时伊朗敦促克制。如今，他们的自信来自实力地位。2025年美国对他们发动打击时，该组织击落了七架美国“收割者”无人机，并险些击中数架战斗机。上个月，他们声称击落了一架由沙特人操作的土耳其制“拜拉克塔尔”无人机。胡塞武装拥有无法被干扰的光纤无人机。该组织过去从伊朗进口成品武器，现在则利用通过阿曼和阿联酋走私或藏在从非洲之角驶出的单桅帆船中的小部件，自行制造大部分武器。一些胡塞无人机几乎可以完全不用伊朗部件制造。“他们能够重新构建受损或被毁的能力——速度远超人们预期，”纽约哥伦比亚大学的彼得·索尔兹伯里表示。地理条件也是优势。反政府武装控制的高地易于防守，尤其是考虑到他们大量使用地雷。他们的领土包括一套此前由军队拥有的洞穴和掩体系统。卫星证据显示这些设施正在扩建。政府军最近缴获了运往胡塞港口的地下隧道掘进设备。这一切都让官方政府感到担忧。沙特或美国的支持可能增强其地面部队的力量。唐纳德·特朗普威胁要对胡塞武装进行“重大军事惩罚”。但代价会很高。胡塞先生津津乐道于也门作为“侵略者坟墓”的名声。他也许会证明自己是对的。■

item.content:encoded:
推动非洲崛起的低调大亨们

中东与非洲 | 非洲公司 从某些方面来看，莫·德瓦吉是个异类。这位魅力非凡的大亨目前是东非唯一的亿万富翁，也是非洲大陆上最年轻的亿万富翁。按照非洲企业巨头们低调的标准，这位51岁的老人却习惯于站在聚光灯下。德瓦吉先生乐于接受采访，包括最近接受《经济学人》的采访。他经常在X上向超过200万粉丝发帖。在其他方面，拥有MeTL集团的德瓦吉先生则是典型代表。MeTL集团是他父亲在20世纪70年代创立的坦桑尼亚企业集团。许多非洲大公司都符合这种多元化、家族所有的模式。本土冠军企业正在崛起。“我们开始看到由非洲人控制的越来越大的企业集团，”麦肯锡非洲区主席阿查·莱克表示。该咨询公司表示，非洲大陆上年营收超过10亿美元的公司中，如今有三分之二为本地所有并在本地设立总部；曾经主导非洲商业的外国跨国公司子公司仅占约30%。从镀金时代的美国到战后的韩国和当代印度，大型本土企业集团都伴随着工业增长而来。因此，这一转变可能是变革性的。

对许多局外人来说，非洲企业的崛起有一张面孔：非洲首富阿利科·丹格特。这位尼日利亚实业家的业务遍及17个非洲国家，从水泥到化肥，他在2023年开设了非洲最大的炼油厂。他计划在肯尼亚建第二座。到2030年，他希望丹格特集团成为非洲第一家千亿美元公司。其他人正紧随其后。在尼日利亚，他面临着一个对手——阿卜杜勒·萨马德·拉比乌，BUA集团的创始人，来自北部城市卡诺的另一个工业王朝的后裔。拉比乌先生与丹格特先生一样，靠水泥以及糖和其他消费品发家，他在5月被列为非洲第二大富豪，当时彭博社估计其净资产约为190亿美元。（此后已降至约140亿美元。）他也有雄心勃勃的扩张计划，例如到2027年将旗下子公司BUA Foods打造成尼日利亚最大的食品制造商。在坦桑尼亚，德瓦吉先生寻求到2030年将MeTL发展成一家价值100亿美元的企业，部分途径是进军采矿和矿产加工领域。他向《经济学人》表示，从长远来看，他希望将其转变为一家电子商务公司。

人们对丹格特先生的关注反映出这样一个事实：像他这样的大型工业企业在非洲仍然罕见。2022年，麦肯锡统计了345家营收超过10亿美元的公司。（如今仅多了26家。）根据最新的《非洲财富报告》——一份对非洲大陆私人财富的年度综述——非洲28位亿万富翁中有25位来自其五大经济体中的四个。“如果你不在尼日利亚、南非或埃及，就很难建立十亿美元级别的企业，”莱克先生说。（第五个是摩洛哥。）由非洲黑人拥有的此类企业更少。在东非，许多最大的公司由亚裔家族拥有，比如坦桑尼亚的德瓦吉家族。在西非，一些最富有的实业家有黎巴嫩血统，其中包括黎巴嫩裔尼日利亚亿万富翁吉尔伯特·沙古里。“非洲人参加资本积累的聚会太晚了，”肯尼亚投资银行家约翰·恩古米指出。亚洲和黎巴嫩家族在殖民统治时期建立的贸易网络使他们占得先机。在直到20世纪80年代都由社会主义者执政的坦桑尼亚，黑人非洲人现在才刚开始追赶上来。

许多人希望效仿丹格特先生。非洲领先的工业企业往往从贸易商做起，然后扩展到制造业和其他领域。多元化的需求部分源于非洲由小而分散的市场拼凑而成。“当你面对一个不够大的经济体时，你最终会做很多种生意，”德瓦吉先生说。他举例说，谷物加工是该地区常见的纵向整合例子：“如果你做小麦加工、玉米加工或大米加工，你需要聚丙烯袋。所以你向后整合进入聚丙烯袋生产。”成功往往取决于与官员的亲密关系。“我想不出有哪个主要实业家不能接触到政府和政策，”加纳智库非洲经济转型中心的弗雷达·约森说。丹格特先生的崛起得益于他与尼日利亚前总统奥卢塞贡·奥巴桑乔的关系，后者的政府出台了有利于他的水泥、糖和大米业务而非外国竞争对手的政策。据了解，拉比乌先生与现任总统博拉·蒂努布关系密切。德瓦吉先生曾是坦桑尼亚执政党的议员。为了避免与政治领导人产生摩擦，许多人选择远离聚光灯。不愿面对媒体的拉比乌先生或许从父亲身上吸取了教训，他父亲在1983年尼日利亚政变后被捕。虽然丹格特先生相对直言不讳，但乔治城大学的肯·奥帕洛表示，他显然“选了一条路”——也就是说，他不插手政治。

分散政治风险的另一种方式是向海外扩张。许多有抱负的“丹格特们”正在这样做。另一位坦桑尼亚巨头罗斯塔姆·阿齐兹在2013年成为该国首位美元亿万富翁，他正在肯尼亚建造他所说的将是非洲最大的液化石油气终端。他表示，未来十年，他将把天然气分销业务“从埃塞俄比亚延伸到南非”。奥帕洛先生指出，得益于东非共同体——非洲最成功的区域集团——各国政府越来越“接受来自边境另一边的公司”，这将对他有所帮助。即便如此，挑战依然存在。一个是高昂的资本成本。在2000年代，坦桑尼亚的银行业规模太小，德瓦吉先生不得不去南非贷款来扩大业务。如今，他指出，“我们有本地银行，也可以在当地获得资本。”信贷正在变得更便宜。但即使是像MeTL这样可以从南非和毛里求斯的银行获得大型银团贷款的大型集团，仍然难以获得负担得起的长期融资。首次公开募股仍然很少见，即使在南非以外也开始出现一些。丹格特先生相对不寻常，因为他将其帝国的一部分在尼日利亚证券交易所上市。非洲上市总市值约为该地区GDP总额的三分之一，而全球为113%，新兴市场平均为61%。部分原因是非洲资本市场仍然很浅，这使企业几乎没有上市的动机。但家族所有者往往也不愿放弃控制权或公开账目供人审视。乌干达企业集团Madhvani集团的尼廷·马德瓦尼指出，在20世纪70年代伊迪·阿明驱逐亚洲人时，他的家族失去了对企业的控制。“我们不想再这样做了，”他说。反过来，外国投资者可能对被认为与国家关系过于密切的非洲公司持谨慎态度。“莫·德瓦吉曾是议员，”坦桑尼亚一家竞争对手企业集团的高管说。“很少有私募股权公司会投资于有这类背景的企业。”

政治仍然是最大的挑战。在一本关于卢旺达经济发展的新书中，曼彻斯特大学的普里蒂什·贝胡里亚认为，政府对本国土著资本家的不信任有助于解释为什么该国产生如此少的自己的大公司。他说，外国资本被视为政治上更安全的选择。这是否是明智的经济选择则不太清楚。尽管丹格特先生取得了企业成就，但在尼日利亚，他的企业尚未启动广泛的工业化。贝胡里亚先生指出，大多数非洲企业集团在提升技术知识方面的投资仍然很少，这使它们没有能力在全球竞争。尽管如此，尼日利亚新兴农业集团Cardinal Torch的大卫·奥卢林表示，为非洲超级大亨增加一点竞争不太可能有害：“你不能只有一个人，却期望出现惊人的增长。”■

订阅《分析非洲》，这是一份每周通讯，让您随时了解这个世界上最年轻——也最不被理解——的大陆。
